path.title: AI for Accounting
path.subtitle: Use AI for the boring 80% — keep the judgment 20% yourself
path.summary: Most CAs are either terrified of AI or embarrassingly trusting of it. Both responses are wrong. This path teaches you exactly which 80 percent of accounting work AI handles well, which 20 percent it cannot touch without burning you, and how to build a defensible workflow that scales your firm without putting your COP number at risk. By the end you can scope an AI engagement for a real client, run a reconciliation pipeline with confidence scores, and explain to a partner why the LLM does not, and will not, sign Form 3CD.

blocks.notesByline: Notes by Anand, articleship batch of 2024

blocks.md:
Two camps of CAs exist right now. Camp One thinks AI will replace them by 2027. Camp Two thinks AI is a glorified autocomplete that gets tax sections wrong. Both camps are wrong, and in opposite ways that cancel out into nothing useful.

Here is the thing nobody puts on a LinkedIn post: AI is not coming for your work; it is coming for the boring 80 percent of your work. The other 20 percent — the judgment, the signature, the conversation with the Assessing Officer — is exactly the part you went through three groups of CA finals to be allowed to do. By the end of this lesson you will have a mental map of which is which, and a vocabulary for explaining it to your partner.

blocks.title: Mental model: a ledger is patterns at scale; AI is a machine for patterns at scale
blocks.md:
Think of every accounting workflow as a pile of repeating patterns: the 12 invoices that look like the 12 from last month; the 47 vendor bills that all share a GSTIN format; the 4,200 bank lines that fall into 22 categories. **A ledger is patterns at scale. AI is a machine for patterns at scale.** The match is structural, not magical.

Once you see this, you stop treating AI as a black box and start treating it like a very fast, very confident articled assistant — one that has read every accounting textbook ever written and absolutely none of your client's GSTIN.

blocks.caption: Watch 4,200 invoice lines flow through the pattern engine; the model groups, scores, flags. The 4,000 it nails fly by; the 200 it isn't sure about glow yellow and queue up for you.

hi-IN.title: Office mein scene yeh hai
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, articled assistant ko bola — "yeh 4,200 entries categorise kar de Monday tak." Monday ko bola — "sir, mujhe mummy se baat karni hai."

AI assistant ko bola — wahi 4,200 entries 14 second mein. Lekin bola: "yaar, 200 mein confident nahi hoon." Yeh confession hi value hai. Tera articled assistant *kabhi* nahi bolega "sir, mujhe doubt hai entry 1,847 pe." Wo silently galat enter karega aur tax audit ke time pakdi jaayegi.

en.title: Same point, no Hindi
en.md: Hand 4,200 entries to a junior on Friday and you'll get them on Wednesday with a 6 percent error rate, undocumented. Hand them to a model and you'll get them in fourteen seconds with a 6 percent flagged-low-confidence rate, fully documented. The honesty itself is the value.

blocks.md:
Here is the first named move you will use for the rest of your career.

**Classify-then-verify.** AI does the first pass — categorising, extracting, matching, with a confidence score on each row. The CA does the second pass — sampling the high-confidence rows, reviewing every low-confidence row, and signing off on the whole.

It is a two-stage workflow. AI's stage is wide and fast; yours is narrow and deep. Done well, you compress what used to be eight hours of articled-assistant work into ninety minutes of senior-level review.

Done badly — meaning you skip the verify step — you ship 4,200 confident-looking categorisations of which 200 are wrong, and you find out at tax audit time. There is no third option.

blocks.title: Classify-then-verify on a real engagement: 4,200 vendor invoices to be tagged with HSN code

steps.label: Step 1 — Standardise input
steps.body: You get 4,200 invoices in 11 different formats. Five minutes of cleanup: one CSV with vendor name, GSTIN, item description, taxable value, GST amount. Don't skip this. Garbage in, confidently wrong out.

steps.label: Step 2 — AI proposes HSN with confidence
steps.body: The model returns: HSN code, 4-digit and 8-digit, plus a confidence score 0 to 100. 3,840 score above 90; 320 between 70 and 90; 40 below 70. Total runtime: 14 seconds for ₹0.42 of API spend.

steps.label: Step 3 — CA samples the easy stuff
steps.body: Pick 50 random rows from the 3,840 high-confidence pile. Verify by hand. If your sample error rate is under 1 percent, accept the pile. If it is higher, you have a systemic problem and you re-prompt.

steps.label: Step 4 — CA reviews the medium pile
steps.body: All 320 medium-confidence rows get a human eye, two seconds each, ten minutes total. You override roughly 40, accept the rest.

steps.label: Step 5 — CA investigates the low pile
steps.body: All 40 low-confidence rows get a real conversation with the file. These are typically genuine ambiguities — composite supplies, mixed packaging, exempt items mis-billed. This is exactly the work a CA is paid for.

steps.label: Step 6 — Eval log
steps.body: Every prompt, every response, every override is logged with timestamps and reviewer name. If a notice arrives in 2028, you can reproduce the entire workflow.

blocks.prompt: In classify-then-verify, what is the worst thing you can do?

choices.label: Skip the verify step on the high-confidence rows entirely
choices.explain: Right. The whole discipline collapses if you skip verification. You don't have to verify every row — that's the point — but you must sample.

choices.label: Sample only 50 of the high-confidence rows instead of all 3,840
choices.explain: Sampling is the design, not a shortcut. 50 is a reasonable sample for a 1 percent error tolerance.

choices.label: Use AI at all for HSN classification
choices.explain: HSN classification at scale is exactly what AI is good at. The judgment call is on the ambiguous 40, not the obvious 3,840.

choices.label: Log the prompt and response
choices.explain: That is the eval log; it is the right thing to do, not the worst.

hi-IN.title: Articled assistant vs AI — honest comparison
hi-IN.md:
Articled assistant: speed slow, accuracy 94%, asks no questions, will quietly mis-tag and disappear.

AI: speed insane, accuracy 96%, flags its own doubts, will tell you exactly which 200 entries it isn't sure about.

Matlab — AI ka biggest superpower hai *honesty*. Articled assistant ka biggest weakness hai *over-confidence*. Yeh ulta lagta hai but yahi sach hai.

en.title: The honesty asymmetry
en.md: AI's superpower is not speed; it is calibrated honesty. A junior won't tell you which entries they guessed. A model will.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The 80/20 split between AI and CA

blocks.md:
Now the bigger picture. Across the full surface of accounting work, roughly 80 percent of the hours are pattern-matching work — extraction, classification, reconciliation, drafting, summarising. Roughly 20 percent is judgment work — choosing accounting policies, signing statutory filings, interpreting a contentious clause, having the conversation with a sceptical client.

AI eats the first 80 percent. You keep the second 20 percent. The question is not whether to use AI; the question is whether you have correctly drawn the line, in writing, for every engagement.

This is the **80/20 split**. The 80 belongs to AI under your supervision. The 20 belongs to you under your signature. There is no overlap and there is no third category.

coach.name: CA-Veteran Vidya
coach.role: Partner, mid-tier Pune firm, 22 years in practice

intro: Hi. I'm Vidya. I run audit and tax at a 14-partner firm in Pune. I've been doing this since before WhatsApp existed, which means I've watched three so-called paradigm shifts come and go.
AI is the fourth. It is also the first one that actually changes how we work. Let me give you six tasks and you tell me which slice they belong to.

scenarios.situation: Extracting GSTINs and invoice numbers from 800 PDF purchase bills.
scenarios.explain: Pure extraction at scale; AI's home turf. Verify totals and a 50-row sample, then proceed.

scenarios.situation: Signing the audit report under Section 143 of the Companies Act.
scenarios.explain: A statutory signature is a CA's personal liability under the Chartered Accountants Act. AI cannot sign. Ever.

scenarios.situation: Drafting a 4-paragraph response to an Income Tax notice based on the assessee's books.
scenarios.explain: Drafting is fine for AI. The CA reviews, edits, and signs. The artefact that goes to the department is the CA's.

scenarios.situation: Deciding whether a litigation provision should be disclosed in financial statements under Ind AS 37.
scenarios.explain: Disclosure judgment requires materiality, management representations, and professional skepticism. AI cannot carry any of those.

scenarios.situation: Categorising 9,000 monthly bank transactions for a 14-outlet restaurant chain into ledger heads.
scenarios.explain: Classify-then-verify. AI does the wide pass; CA reviews low-confidence and high-rupee entries.

scenarios.situation: Choosing between two competing accounting policies for revenue recognition on a long-term project.
scenarios.explain: Policy choice is judgment under the relevant standard plus client context. AI may surface options; the choice is the CA's.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the third-category fantasy
blocks.md: Every CA, on first contact with AI, tries to invent a third category — "AI does it but a human spot-checks" or "AI signs and the CA reviews afterwards." There is no third category. **Either AI does it under your supervision, or you do it. The signature is yours either way.** Anything that blurs this line is how firms get into trouble.

blocks.prompt: Order these activities to set up an AI-assisted workflow for a new client engagement, from first to last.

items.label: Define the 80/20 split for this specific engagement, in writing
items.detail: Which tasks AI handles, which the CA handles, with named confidence thresholds.

items.label: Standardise input data into a single rectangular format
items.detail: One CSV per data type, consistent headers, no merged cells.

items.label: Build and version-control the prompt with required output schema
items.detail: JSON output with every required field; reject responses that don't match.

items.label: Run AI on the data with confidence scoring
items.detail: Get back categorised output plus per-row confidence.

items.label: Apply the verify tier — sample high-confidence, review medium, investigate low
items.detail: This is the irreducible human step.

items.label: Save the eval log: prompt, response, reviewer, overrides, model version
items.detail: Audit trail must be reproducible for the retention period.

blocks.instruction: Take this engagement and write the 80/20 split as a 6-line list. The brief: a Surat textile exporter wants you to handle their monthly compliance — vendor invoice booking (~600/month), bank reconciliation, GST return preparation, TDS computation and challan, and the year-end balance sheet. Mark each as AI-led or CA-only and write one sentence on why.

blocks.expected:
## 80/20 split — Surat textile client

1. Vendor invoice booking — **AI-led**, classify-then-verify with confidence scoring; CA samples high-confidence, reviews low-confidence and any entry above ₹2 lakh.
2. Bank reconciliation — **AI-led**, fuzzy matching with confidence; CA reviews unmatched and any forex transaction.
3. GST return preparation — **AI-led drafting, CA-only signoff**; AI populates GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B drafts from books, CA reviews and files.
4. TDS computation — **AI-led** with rate lookup via RAG against the Income Tax Act; CA verifies threshold applicability and treaty position for any non-resident payment.
5. TDS challan filing — **CA-only**; statutory filing, never automated, never AI-shipped.
6. Year-end balance sheet — **CA-only on classification and disclosure judgment**; AI may produce first-pass schedules and tie-outs, CA chooses policy and signs.

blocks.prompt: Which of these are signs that you have **correctly** drawn the 80/20 line for an engagement? (Select all that apply.)

choices.label: Each task is explicitly tagged AI-led or CA-only in the engagement letter
choices.explain: Right. If it is not in writing, the line will move under pressure.

choices.label: The CA can name the confidence threshold for every AI-led task
choices.explain: Right. 'High confidence' is a useless label; '95% or above accepted, below sampled' is a workflow.

choices.label: There is a third category called 'AI signs but CA reviews after'
choices.explain: There is no such category. The signature is the CA's; AI never signs anything.

choices.label: The engagement promises to be 'fully AI-automated'
choices.explain: If your engagement promises full automation, you have not drawn the line; you have erased it.

hi-IN.title: Tea-break disclaimer
hi-IN.md:
Office mein partner ne pucha — "AI hai toh kya articled assistants ki zaroorat hi nahi rahi?"

Galat sawaal. Articled assistants ki zaroorat ab *judgment* ke liye hai, photocopy ke liye nahi. Jis articled assistant ko sirf data entry aati hai, uska future short hai. Jo low-confidence row pe ruk ke poochta hai "sir, yeh composite supply hai ya mixed?" — uska future bahut lambha hai.

en.title: What changes for juniors
en.md: Articled assistants are not obsolete; the data-entry job is. The judgment job — investigating the 40 low-confidence rows AI flagged — is now their actual training ground. The good ones welcome it.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 12 Lakh Rows, 31 Hours Saved, 6% Still Yours
blocks.source: Audit manager at Kothari Joshi & Associates, a Mumbai mid-tier CA firm with 84 staff
blocks.story:
In November 2025, the firm took on the FY24-25 statutory audit of a Vile Parle FMCG distributor doing **₹312 crore turnover** across 1,400 SKUs and 19 warehouses. The general ledger came in at **12,04,387 rows** — three articled assistants, six weeks at planned utilisation, ₹4.8 lakh of write-down already baked into the engagement budget.

The partner had been quietly piloting a classify-then-verify pipeline. They pointed it at the ledger with a 23-category chart-of-accounts mapping. **94.1% of rows came back high-confidence (above 0.85), 5.9% needed CA review** — about 71,000 rows in the review queue, sorted by confidence ascending.

The articled assistants worked the queue, not the whole ledger. They closed the categorisation in **9 days instead of 6 weeks**. The partner's review of the high-confidence stratum (a 2,400-row stratified sample) caught **17 misclassifications** — all in one cluster: the AI had been confidently mapping 'sales return — damaged goods' as 'sales return — quality reject'. Material to nobody, but the partner flagged it for the FY25-26 retraining set.

**Net: 31 hours saved per month of bookkeeping support across the engagement; ₹2.1 lakh of recovered margin; one new pattern caught that would have shipped silently the year before.**
blocks.takeaway: AI does the wide-and-fast 94%. You do the narrow-and-deep 6%. Skip the 6% and you have not innovated, you have just ratified the model's mistakes at speed.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Day 1 of the AI Rollout — Scope the 80/20
blocks.setup:
It is **Monday, 10 February 2026, 9:42 AM**. You are **Anand, second-year articleship at Bharat & Co.**, a Pune mid-size CA firm with 47 SME clients. Your senior partner, **Pramod**, just walked into the conference room holding a printout of last quarter's WIP report.

*'Anand. We are losing margin on bookkeeping. The juniors hate it, the seniors won't touch it, and the clients think we are slow. I want you to scope the firm's AI rollout. 90 days. Bookkeeping first. Tell me where we start, where we do not, and what could go wrong.'*

He slides the printout across. 47 clients. Turnover from ₹40 lakh kirana shops to a ₹180 crore auto-parts manufacturer. You have until end-of-day to come back with a scope.

coach.name: Partner Pramod
coach.role: Senior partner, 22 years post-qualification, runs the audit and assurance practice

stages.prompt: **Stage 1.** Pramod asks the obvious first question. *'Which clients do we start with?'* What is your move?

options.label: Start with the ₹180 crore auto-parts manufacturer. Biggest fee, biggest impact, biggest signal to the rest of the firm.
options.explain: Wrong starting point. The ₹180 crore client has the most complex chart of accounts, the most regulator-facing artefacts, and the most expensive failure mode. Pilot risk is upside-down. You want a forgiving pilot, not a heroic one.

options.label: Pick 6 to 8 mid-sized clients (₹15 to ₹60 crore turnover) with clean ledgers, single-state GST registration, and a CA-side relationship manager who is willing to co-pilot.
options.explain: **Correct.** Mid-sized clients give you statistical signal (enough rows to test confidence thresholds), low blast radius (failure does not threaten the firm), and a relationship manager who can review the AI output without panicking. This is the textbook pilot cohort.

options.label: Run it across all 47 clients in parallel. The model needs scale to learn.
options.explain: You are not training a foundation model. You are deploying a workflow. Running 47 simultaneous pilots means 47 simultaneous failure modes, no single owner, and Pramod fielding 47 angry calls. Hard pass.

options.label: Start with the ₹40 lakh kirana shops. Simple ledgers, lowest stakes.
options.explain: Too small. Their ledgers are too sparse to test confidence thresholds, their fees do not justify the engineering investment, and you will conclude 'AI works' on data that is not representative. Pilot has to look like the production target.

stages.prompt: **Stage 2.** Pramod nods. Now: *'What does the AI do, and what does the CA do?'* Draw the line.

options.label: AI categorises every transaction. CA reviews the final P&L for reasonableness. Done.
options.explain: P&L-level review will not catch the systematic misclassifications that hurt at audit. You need stratified row-level review on the low-confidence tier and sampled review on the high-confidence tier. P&L review is a back-stop, not the primary.

options.label: AI does first-pass categorisation with a confidence score per row. CA reviews 100% of low-confidence rows (below threshold) and a stratified sample of high-confidence rows.
options.explain: **This is classify-then-verify.** AI is wide and fast; CA is narrow and deep. The threshold is a parameter you tune; sampling rate is a parameter you tune. Both stay in CA hands. Pramod will recognise this from his own articleship — it is the audit-sampling logic, just applied to bookkeeping.

options.label: AI proposes categorisations, CA accepts or rejects each one in a UI. 100% human review of every row.
options.explain: Now you have just added a click to existing manual work. No time saved. No margin recovered. The whole point of AI is to compress the volume the CA has to touch. Reviewing every row defeats the purpose.

options.label: AI categorises, CA only intervenes if a client complaint surfaces.
options.explain: No. This is the 'rubber-stamp without even rubber-stamping' workflow. By the time a client complains, the audit working papers are already wrong. CA review is upstream of the artefact, not downstream of the complaint.

stages.prompt: **Stage 3.** Pramod's eyes narrow. *'And when something goes wrong — and it will — how do we know it was the AI and not the junior?'* What do you propose?

options.label: We will trust the team to flag issues in the morning huddle.
options.explain: Memory-based defence collapses under regulatory pressure. Two years from now an ICAI inquiry will ask 'what did the AI propose, what did the human change, when'. 'We discussed it in a huddle' is not an answer.

options.label: Append-only eval log: every AI categorisation, the row hash, model version, confidence score, who reviewed it, what they changed, timestamp. Retained per the 7-year tax record rule.
options.explain: **Yes.** This is the precondition, not the nice-to-have. Pramod will sleep better knowing that any AI-touched artefact can be reconstructed end-to-end. Two database tables, some middleware, and a retention policy. Boring infrastructure, indispensable.

options.label: Screenshots saved to the engagement folder.
options.explain: Screenshots are not queryable, not append-only, and not standardised. They are evidence theatre, not an audit trail. Pramod will see through it the moment he asks 'show me every AI-touched journal entry above ₹50,000 last quarter'.

options.label: Trust the AI vendor's logs.
options.explain: The AI vendor's logs are written by the AI vendor, retained per the AI vendor's policy, queryable on the AI vendor's terms. Your audit defence cannot live on someone else's server. Own your eval log.

stages.prompt: **Stage 4.** Pramod asks the question every partner asks. *'What is the failure mode that scares you the most?'*

options.label: The AI gets a row wrong.
options.explain: Individual wrong rows are expected and survivable — that is what the review tier exists for. The scary failure modes are systematic, not individual.

options.label: Systematic misclassification that the CA review samples miss because every row in the cluster looks confident. Caught at audit. Material restatement.
options.explain: **This is the right fear.** A confident-looking 6,000-row cluster mapped to the wrong head of expense will sail through any reasonable sample. Mitigation: stratify samples by category, not just by confidence. Re-test sampled categories quarterly. Pramod will recognise this — it is the audit assertion-and-population problem, dressed in new clothes.

options.label: The AI vendor goes out of business.
options.explain: Real risk, but a procurement and continuity question, not the scariest workflow failure. Mitigate by keeping prompts and evals portable. Not your top fear today.

options.label: Junior staff over-trust the AI and stop learning.
options.explain: **Also legitimate, and Pramod will love that you flagged it.** If juniors learn to click 'accept' on AI output without ever doing the reasoning, in five years your firm has no senior CAs. Mitigation: rotate juniors through manual categorisation on a sampled basis; make them defend their accept/reject decisions in review. Half-credit for systematic-misclassification, full-credit if you raise both.

outcomes.perfect: Pramod sits back and says *'Draft the 90-day plan by Friday. You are leading the rollout.'* You picked the right pilot cohort, drew the classify-then-verify line in the right place, demanded an eval log on day one, and named both the systematic-misclassification and skill-atrophy risks. This is the scoping conversation a partner wishes every articled assistant could have.
outcomes.good: Pramod is satisfied but takes the pen from you on one or two answers. You have the right instincts on classify-then-verify, but re-read the lesson on confidence-stratified sampling and the eval log. The 90-day plan is yours to write; come back next Monday with v2.
outcomes.learn: Pramod is patient but firm. *'Anand, this is not a deployment, this is a discipline. Re-read the lesson, especially the sections on classify-then-verify, the review tiers, and why the eval log is the precondition not the postscript. We will have this conversation again on Wednesday.'* The good news: he is willing to have it again. The next firm might not be.

points: A ledger is patterns at scale; AI is a machine for patterns at scale; the match is structural, not magical.
Classify-then-verify: AI does the wide first pass with confidence scores; the CA does the deep second pass on flagged rows and high-rupee entries.
Roughly 80 percent of accounting hours are pattern-matching work AI eats; roughly 20 percent are judgment hours only a CA may sign.
There is no third category. Either AI does it under your supervision, or you do it; the signature is yours either way.
AI's biggest superpower is calibrated honesty — it tells you which rows it is unsure about. A junior never will.

blocks.prompt: Pick one engagement you currently handle. Write the 80/20 split for it as a 6 to 10 line list, marking each task AI-led or CA-only with a one-sentence reason. Where did you find yourself wanting to invent a third category, and what did that pressure tell you?

blocks.md:
Prompting for blog posts is forgiving. If a model writes "the cat sat on the mat" instead of "the cat slept on the mat," the world keeps turning. Prompting for financial work is unforgiving. If a model writes ₹14,82,000 instead of ₹14,28,000, your client pays the wrong tax.

The difference is not subtle. Text errors are stylistic; number errors are material. By the end of this lesson you will have two named moves that catch the model before the client sees the damage.

blocks.title: Mental model: numbers are not text — verify every figure
blocks.md:
When a model produces text, errors are usually obvious or harmless — wrong tone, missed nuance, awkward phrasing. When a model produces numbers, errors are usually invisible and material. **A number that is wrong by one digit looks identical to a number that is right.**

So: every prompt that asks for a number must also ask for the source, and every output must be reconciled to a total. No exceptions, no shortcuts. The number is the artefact; everything else is workflow.

blocks.caption: Watch a 47-line invoice extract: AI returns the table, then the totals from the source and the totals from the AI output line up side by side. The 14-rupee mismatch glows red instantly.

hi-IN.title: Office story — comma ka kahar
hi-IN.md:
Articled ne ChatGPT ko bola — "is invoice ka total nikaal". AI ne bola — Rs. 14,28,000.

Client ne dekha — "haan sahi hai". Submission ke baad realise hua — invoice mein actual total tha Rs. 14,82,000. Comma place change ho gaya tha. ₹54,000 ka ITC chala gaya kyunki vendor ka GSTIN mismatched ho gaya tha aur reconciliation pe pakda nahi.

Bhai — number aur text alag chiz hai. Text mein typo dikhta hai. Number mein typo *paisa* hai.

en.title: The lakh comma trap
en.md: An LLM cheerfully returned ₹14,28,000 as a total. The actual figure was ₹14,82,000. Two digits swapped, comma placement identical, ₹54,000 of ITC marooned. With text, a typo is visible. With numbers, a typo is money.

blocks.md:
First named move. Stop asking for paragraphs. Start asking for JSON.

A **structured-output prompt** specifies, in the prompt itself, the exact shape of the response: every field, every type, every required key. The model returns JSON that either parses cleanly into your schema or fails loudly. Free-form prose hides errors; structured output exposes them.

In practice this means: instead of "summarise this purchase invoice," you write "return JSON with exactly these keys: vendor_name (string), gstin (15-character string), invoice_number (string), invoice_date (YYYY-MM-DD), taxable_value (number, rupees), igst (number, rupees), cgst (number, rupees), sgst (number, rupees), total (number, rupees). If a field is missing, return null. Do not include any text outside the JSON object."

Notice what changed. The model can no longer slip in a hedged summary or invent a category; the schema is the contract.

blocks.title: Building a structured-output prompt for vendor invoice extraction

steps.label: Step 1 — Define the schema first
steps.body: Before you write a single English word, write the JSON schema. Field names, types, required vs optional, format constraints (GSTIN is exactly 15 chars, dates are YYYY-MM-DD).

steps.label: Step 2 — Wrap with a system prompt that demands strict adherence
steps.body: 'You return JSON only. No prose, no markdown fences, no explanation. If a field cannot be extracted, return null. If the document is not a tax invoice, return {"error": "not_invoice"}.'

steps.label: Step 3 — Add a citation field
steps.body: Include a 'source_lines' array — the line numbers in the source document where each value came from. This is the audit trail at the row level.

steps.label: Step 4 — Include 1 or 2 examples
steps.body: Few-shot examples beat instructions. Show the model one good input/output pair. Watch the consistency improve immediately.

steps.label: Step 5 — Validate on parse
steps.body: Your code attempts to parse the JSON. If it fails — missing field, wrong type, GSTIN of wrong length — re-prompt or flag. Never silently accept malformed output.

steps.label: Step 6 — Reconcile totals before trusting
steps.body: Sum extracted taxable + IGST + CGST + SGST and compare with the model's 'total' field and the source-document total. If they don't match within ₹1, the row is flagged.

blocks.prompt: Why is structured output better than free-form prose for financial extraction?

choices.label: Because the schema is a contract — malformed output fails loudly instead of silently containing errors
choices.explain: Right. Free-form output looks fine even when it is wrong. Structured output either parses or doesn't.

choices.label: Because LLMs are faster on JSON
choices.explain: Slightly true on tokenisation; not the point.

choices.label: Because JSON looks more professional in client decks
choices.explain: The point is verifiability, not aesthetics.

choices.label: Because structured output costs less
choices.explain: Cost is incidental; some structured prompts use more tokens because of the schema description.

hi-IN.title: Schema = engagement letter
hi-IN.md:
Sochta hu — JSON schema basically engagement letter ka chhota version hai. Pehle clearly likh diya — "yeh deliverable, yeh format, yeh fields". Phir AI ko deliver karna padta hai uss exact contract pe.

Bina schema ke prompt — "summarise this" — woh same hai jaise client ko bolna "kuch karke do". Dono cases mein kuch bhi mil sakta hai.

en.title: Schema as engagement letter
en.md: Think of the schema as the engagement letter for the model. "Summarise this" is the equivalent of "do something useful." The schema makes the deliverable enforceable.

blocks.md:
Second named move. For every figure the model produces, demand a citation back to the source.

The **show your sources demand** is a single line in your prompt: *'For every value, also return the page number, line number, or row reference in the source document where you read it.'* The model now produces extracted values *plus* a pointer back to the original. You spot-check the pointer; if the pointer is wrong or fabricated, you discard the value.

This catches three failure modes at once. One: the model invented the number from training data instead of reading it. Two: the model read the wrong row. Three: the model averaged or interpreted when you wanted a literal extract.

For reading PDFs, ask for page + line. For Excel, ask for sheet + cell address. For long contracts, ask for clause number. The model will sometimes refuse or invent a citation; both are useful failure signals.

coach.role: Partner, mid-tier Pune firm, 22 years in practice

intro: Right. You've seen the moves; now tell me how you'd handle a few prompts that landed on my desk last month.
For each one, decide whether the prompt is safe to run as-is or whether you'd rewrite it before letting an articled assistant use it.

scenarios.situation: 'Read this invoice and tell me the total.'
scenarios.explain: No structure, no citation, no schema. Could return any of three plausible numbers depending on parsing. Rewrite as a structured-output prompt with source line citation.

scenarios.situation: 'Return JSON with keys vendor, gstin (15 chars), taxable (number), igst (number), cgst (number), sgst (number), total (number), source_lines (array). Verify total = taxable + igst + cgst + sgst before returning.'
scenarios.explain: Schema, types, validation, citation request. This is what a real production prompt looks like. Ship it (with parsing on your end).

scenarios.situation: 'Summarise the financials of this annual report in 200 words.'
scenarios.explain: This is a text task, not a number-extraction task. Free-form prose is acceptable; the deliverable is a summary, not a figure to file. Different discipline.

scenarios.situation: 'What is the GST rate on solar panels? Give me the section number.'
scenarios.explain: Asks the model to answer from training data with no source. Rewrite with RAG over the actual GST notifications, and demand a verbatim quote.

scenarios.situation: 'Extract the closing balance for cash from this trial balance and tell me the line number you read it from.'
scenarios.explain: Specific task, citation requirement, single value. Tight enough to ship after a one-row sanity check.

scenarios.situation: 'You're a senior CA. Tell me how to handle the ITC mismatch.'
scenarios.explain: Role-play prompts on judgment topics produce confident-sounding generic advice. Rewrite to ask for options surfaced from CBIC circulars with citations, then exercise CA judgment yourself.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the well-formatted hallucination
blocks.md:
The most dangerous output is one that *looks* right. Clean tables, neat columns, GSTINs that pass format validation — and one number that is silently wrong by ₹54,000.

**Format quality and number quality are uncorrelated.** A model that produces beautiful JSON can still invent the IGST. The defence is reconciliation, not aesthetics.

blocks.prompt: You're processing 800 vendor invoices for a client. Order these prompt-engineering steps from first to last.

items.label: Define the JSON output schema with field types and constraints
items.detail: Vendor name (string), GSTIN (15 chars), taxable value (number), etc.

items.label: Add 1 to 2 worked examples (input → expected output) to the prompt
items.detail: Few-shot examples beat instructions for consistency.

items.label: Add the 'show your sources' demand for every numeric field
items.detail: Each value carries a back-pointer to the source line/page/cell.

items.label: Add the system instruction: 'JSON only, no prose; null for missing fields'
items.detail: Removes any temptation for the model to slip in commentary.

items.label: Run on a 10-invoice pilot and validate parsing + reconciliation
items.detail: Catch schema mismatches and totals errors on a small set first.

items.label: Run on the full 800 with logging of every prompt, response, and override
items.detail: The eval log captures the full trail.

blocks.prompt: Which of these are good practices for prompts that extract numbers? (Select all that apply.)

choices.label: Demand JSON output with explicit field types
choices.explain: Right. Schemas catch structural errors at parse time.

choices.label: Demand a source citation (page/line/cell) for every numeric value
choices.explain: Right. Citations turn invisible errors into visible ones.

choices.label: Trust the output if the formatting looks neat
choices.explain: Wrong. Format quality and number quality are uncorrelated. Neat output can still be wrong.

choices.label: Reconcile extracted totals against the source-document total before trusting
choices.explain: Right. The reconciliation is the only thing standing between you and a comma-displacement disaster.

hi-IN.title: Articled assistant ka golden rule, AI ke liye bhi
hi-IN.md:
Senior ne hamesha bola tha — "figure de raha hai toh source bata." Trial balance se number nikaal ke aaye toh page number, ledger book ka line number, kuch toh chahiye.

Vahi rule AI ke liye. Number bata raha hai toh source dikha. Source nahi hai toh trust nahi hai.

en.title: The same rule, applied to a different junior
en.md: Every senior teaches the same lesson on day one: if you give me a number, give me the source. The rule applies cleanly to AI; the only thing that changes is how fast you can demand it.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The ₹2.4 Crore Line Item That Did Not Exist
blocks.source: Engagement partner at Mehta Iyer & Co., a Hyderabad CA firm with a strong manufacturing client base
blocks.story:
On 11 October 2025, a first-year articleship — bright, eager, six weeks in — was asked to produce a one-page board summary of the September P&L for a client with **₹91 crore turnover** in industrial coatings. The client's CFO wanted it by 6 PM the same day for a 9 AM Sunday board call.

The junior pasted the raw trial balance into a chat interface and typed a single line: *'Summarise this P&L for a board pack. One page.'*

The AI obliged. The output read beautifully. Crisp narrative, clean variance commentary, three-bullet executive summary. Tucked into the cost-of-goods-sold breakdown, between 'raw materials' and 'consumables', sat a line: **'Forex hedging losses — ₹2,41,38,000'**.

The client did not run a forex hedging programme. The line item did not exist anywhere in the trial balance. The model had constructed a plausible-looking fabrication because the surrounding context (an exporter, a quarter of dollar weakness, a P&L in rupees) made forex hedging losses statistically reasonable. **It was a hallucinated line item with a hallucinated rupee figure.**

The junior did not catch it. The senior reviewer, time-pressed, did not catch it. The engagement partner caught it at 5:47 PM during her 13-minute final read, only because she happened to remember the client did not hedge. **₹13 minutes between fabrication and the boardroom.**

The firm now mandates structured-output prompts (JSON schema, fixed keys) and source-citation lines (every figure must point back to a trial balance row) for all AI-assisted client deliverables. The junior, to her credit, helped write the new policy.
blocks.takeaway: Free-form prose hides hallucinations. JSON schemas expose them. If the model has to fill a fixed key, it cannot smuggle in a fictional one.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Write the P&L Summary Prompt — Without the Hallucinations
blocks.setup:
It is **Tuesday, 17 March 2026, 4:15 PM**. **Anand** is back at his desk. The 90-day rollout is in week 5; the pilot cohort is humming. Now **Senior-CA Sundari** — a 9-years-post-qual senior who runs the bookkeeping practice for the pilot clients — has dropped a problem on his desk.

*'Anand. We are doing monthly P&L summaries for 8 pilot clients. The current prompt is one line: "Summarise the September P&L". Last month the AI invented a deferred-revenue figure for a client that runs cash-only retail. CFO almost asked us about it on a call. I want you to design a structured-output prompt by EOD. I want JSON, I want citations, I want it to fail loudly when the data is missing — not quietly invent.'*

She puts a coffee on his desk. *'Walk me through it stage by stage. I want to learn this with you.'*

coach.name: Senior-CA Sundari
coach.role: Senior CA, 9 years post-qualification, runs bookkeeping for the AI pilot cohort

stages.prompt: **Stage 1.** Sundari asks: *'Why is "summarise this P&L" a bad prompt? Be specific.'*

options.label: It is too short. Just make it longer.
options.explain: Length is not the issue. A 50-word prompt that says 'summarise this P&L in detail' is just as broken. The problem is structural, not verbose-vs-terse.

options.label: It does not specify the output shape, the required fields, or the source of truth. The model is free to interpret, free to invent line items, and free to hide the inventions inside fluent prose.
options.explain: **Exactly.** A free-form prompt invites a free-form output. The model has no contractual obligation to stick to the trial balance, so it doesn't. Sundari nods — this is the diagnosis you wanted to lead with.

options.label: It does not say 'do not hallucinate'.
options.explain: Telling a model 'do not hallucinate' is like telling a child 'do not be tired'. It is a behavioural plea, not a structural fix. The model will hallucinate anyway; it just won't know it has.

options.label: It uses the word 'summarise'. We should say 'analyse'.
options.explain: Vocabulary swap does not solve the problem. 'Analyse this P&L' has the same failure mode as 'summarise this P&L' — both leave the output shape and source-of-truth unspecified.

stages.prompt: **Stage 2.** Sundari nods. *'Now design the output schema. What does the JSON look like?'* Pick the best version.

options.label: `{ "summary": "...", "highlights": ["..."] }` — flexible, lets the model decide what to surface.
options.explain: Two free-form string fields. You have changed the wrapper but not the contract. The model will write a paragraph in 'summary' and a list of paragraphs in 'highlights', and the hallucinations come right back. Schema by name only.

options.label: Fixed keys for every line of the standard P&L: `revenue`, `cogs`, `gross_profit`, `opex_breakdown` (with named sub-keys: `salaries`, `rent`, `utilities`, `professional_fees`, `other`), `ebitda`, `depreciation`, `interest`, `tax`, `pat`. Every value is a number in rupees plus a `source_row_id` pointing back to the trial balance row.
options.explain: **This is the move.** Every key is named. Every value has a source pointer. If the model wants to invent 'forex hedging losses' it has nowhere to put it — the schema does not have that key, and even if you added an `other` key, that key requires a `source_row_id`. Sundari smiles.

options.label: One key: `narrative` (string, max 500 words).
options.explain: You have just put a word limit on the hallucination. The fabrication still happens; it is now 500 words instead of 800. The structural problem is unsolved.

options.label: Fixed keys but no source pointers — pointers slow the model down and cost extra tokens.
options.explain: Tokens cost paise. A wrong board pack costs the engagement. The source pointer is the verifiability layer; it is the difference between a draft you can audit and a draft you have to take on faith. Skip it and you have skipped the only thing that catches fabrication.

stages.prompt: **Stage 3.** *'Now the failure modes. What does the prompt say when the data is missing or ambiguous?'* What instruction goes in?

options.label: *'If a value is missing, estimate it based on prior periods.'*
options.explain: You have just instructed the model to fabricate, in writing. This is the prompt-engineering equivalent of telling a junior 'if you can't find the receipt, just guess'. Catastrophic.

options.label: *'If a value cannot be derived from the supplied trial balance with a clear source row, return null for the field and add the field name to a top-level `missing_fields` array. Do not estimate, do not interpolate, do not infer from other periods.'*
options.explain: **Yes.** Failure has to be loud, structured, and localised. A null field plus a `missing_fields` array means the reviewer sees, at a glance, what the model could not source. No silent invention. Sundari is taking notes.

options.label: *'Do your best.'*
options.explain: 'Do your best' is permission to invent. Sundari sighs.

options.label: *'Flag low-confidence values with a 🤔 emoji.'*
options.explain: Cute. Not parseable. The CA reviewer's eye will skim past an emoji; a structured `missing_fields` array forces a programmatic check before the file is opened. Use mechanism, not vibes.

stages.prompt: **Stage 4.** *'Last piece. The prompt is built. The output JSON arrives. What is the one human verification step you will not skip?'*

options.label: Spot-check 3 random source-row pointers against the actual trial balance row. If any pointer is wrong or fabricated, reject the entire output and re-run.
options.explain: **Correct.** The pointer is the contract. If even one pointer is wrong, you have evidence the model is willing to fabricate the citation layer too — at which point every other figure is suspect. Three checks take 90 seconds and cost almost nothing.

options.label: Read the narrative summary at the bottom and check it 'sounds right'.
options.explain: 'Sounds right' is exactly how the ₹2.41 crore phantom forex line in Mehta Iyer's case slipped through. Plausibility is not verification. The narrative will always sound right; the model is good at narratives.

options.label: Run the output through a second AI for a 'consistency check'.
options.explain: Two models that share training data will share blind spots. You have not added independence; you have added another opaque layer. Use a human and a deterministic rule (does row_id_X exist in the trial balance, yes/no), not another model.

options.label: Check that the totals tie: revenue minus cogs equals gross profit, gross profit minus opex equals ebitda, and so on down the P&L.
options.explain: **Also correct, also non-negotiable.** Arithmetic ties are the cheapest deterministic check available. They catch a whole class of failures — copy-paste errors, double-counted rows, dropped sub-totals — that pointer checks miss. Half-credit for one, full-credit for both.

outcomes.perfect: Sundari leans back. *'Anand, write this up. We are using your prompt across the pilot starting Monday.'* You diagnosed the free-form-prompt failure mode, designed a fixed-key schema with source pointers, made failure loud and structured, and named the two non-negotiable verification steps. This is what 'AI as a tool' actually looks like in a CA practice — not a chatbot, a contract.
outcomes.good: Sundari is happy with most of it but pulls you up on one or two answers. You have the structural intuition; re-read the lesson on the show-your-sources demand and the difference between estimating and sourcing. Bring v2 of the prompt by Thursday.
outcomes.learn: Sundari is firm. *'Anand, the difference between a useful AI prompt and a dangerous one is whether it can fabricate without you noticing. Re-read the lesson — the structured-output move and the show-your-sources demand. We will rewrite this together tomorrow.'* The Mehta Iyer story is in the textbook for a reason; do not be the next case study.

points: Numbers are not text. A wrong number looks identical to a right one; verification is non-negotiable.
Structured-output prompts make the schema a contract: malformed responses fail at parse time instead of in production.
The 'show your sources' demand turns invisible errors into visible ones; demand page/line/cell for every figure.
Format quality and number quality are uncorrelated; neat output can still be wrong by ₹54,000.
Always reconcile extracted totals against the source-document total before trusting any row.

blocks.prompt: Take one prompt you (or your team) currently use for any financial extraction or summarisation task. Rewrite it as a structured-output prompt with a JSON schema and a source-citation demand. What did you have to make explicit that was previously left implicit?

blocks.notesByline: Notes by Anand, articleship batch of 2024

blocks.md:
Bank reconciliation is the activity that articled assistants think defines accounting. A 14,000-line statement, a 14,000-line ledger, and the patient question: which line on each side corresponds to which line on the other? It used to take three days. With AI, it takes three hours, and most of those three hours are you being a CA instead of a sorter.

But only if you do it right. Most firms doing AI reconciliation today are doing it the wrong way — exact-match-only against text strings, no confidence scoring, no review tier — and quietly missing 6 to 12 percent of the matches that a careful pattern-matcher would have caught.

blocks.title: Mental model: reconciliation is fuzzy matching at scale
blocks.md:
Stop thinking of reconciliation as a sorting problem. Start thinking of it as a **fuzzy matching** problem.

The bank says "NEFT/RPL/2,40,000". The ledger says "Repl Industries — 2,40,000". A human knows these are the same transaction; an exact-string match misses it; a fuzzy matcher catches it because the date matches, the amount matches, and there is a partial-name overlap.

**AI is, structurally, a fuzzy matcher.** Reconciliation is, structurally, fuzzy matching. The two were waiting for each other.

blocks.caption: A 14,000-line bank statement and a 14,000-line ledger flow into the matcher. Watch the confidence-scored output emerge in three colour-coded streams: high, medium, low. The low stream queues up for human review.

hi-IN.title: Bank narration ka kavita problem
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, Indian bank narration kavita hoti hai. Same vendor, same amount, har month alag spelling.

Month 1: 'NEFT-N123-RAJ ENT'  
Month 2: 'RTGS/RAJ ENTERPRISES'  
Month 3: 'IMPS-RAJ ENTERPRIS' (truncated, comma katwa diya)  
Month 4: 'NEFT-RAJ ENT PVT LTD'

Exception-based matching ke liye yeh nightmare hai. AI ke liye yeh sirf Tuesday hai. Embedding similarity 0.92 — same vendor, ship the match, move on.

en.title: The narration poetry problem
en.md: Indian bank narrations vary every month for the same vendor — abbreviations, truncations, channel codes, capitalisation. Exact matching gives up. A model that does embedding similarity does not.

blocks.md:
First named move. Stop producing binary match/no-match outputs. Start producing **confidence-scored matches**.

A confidence-scored match is a triple: (bank line, ledger line, score from 0 to 100). The score reflects how strongly the matcher believes these two lines are the same transaction, based on amount equality (high weight), date proximity (medium), narration similarity (variable), and reference number overlap when present.

By outputting scores instead of binaries, you turn a 14,000-line opaque match into a triaged worklist. You can now say: above 95, accept (with sampling). Between 70 and 95, eyeball. Below 70, treat as unmatched and investigate. The threshold is yours to set; the score is the model's job.

blocks.title: What confidence-scored matching looks like in practice (a 14,000-line bank rec for a Bangalore restaurant chain)

steps.label: Step 1 — Load both sides into a common schema
steps.body: Bank: date, amount, narration, channel. Ledger: date, amount, party, narration. One row per transaction; no merged cells, no totals rows.

steps.label: Step 2 — Score every plausible pair on amount + date + similarity
steps.body: For each bank line, the matcher considers ledger lines within ±3 days and ±0 rupees, scores narration similarity, and returns top-3 candidate matches with scores.

steps.label: Step 3 — Pick the best match per row, score 0 to 100
steps.body: Of the 14,000 bank lines: 12,400 score above 95, 1,200 score between 70 and 95, 320 score below 70, 80 have no candidate (unmatched on the bank side).

steps.label: Step 4 — Accept-zone sampling
steps.body: Sample 100 random matches from the 12,400 high-confidence pile. Verify each by hand. Sample error rate: 0.3 percent. Acceptable; accept the pile.

steps.label: Step 5 — Review zone, row by row
steps.body: All 1,200 medium-confidence matches reviewed at roughly 5 seconds each — 100 minutes. Override rate: about 8 percent. Pattern: most overrides are near-duplicate vendor names that need a manual disambiguation.

steps.label: Step 6 — Investigate zone
steps.body: All 320 low-confidence and 80 unmatched lines get a real conversation with the file. About 60 percent are timing differences (cleared in next month), 30 percent are missing ledger entries (booking errors), 10 percent are genuine reconciling items requiring follow-up.

steps.label: Step 7 — Eval log + signoff
steps.body: Full match table with scores, override log, and unresolved exceptions go into the working papers. Partner reviews exception list, signs off, files.

blocks.prompt: What is the right way to handle the high-confidence pile in a confidence-scored reconciliation?

choices.label: Sample a random subset and verify by hand; accept the pile if sample error rate is acceptable
choices.explain: Right. Sampling is the audit-grade discipline; full review of high-confidence rows defeats the time savings.

choices.label: Skip review entirely — that's why they're high-confidence
choices.explain: Skipping all review of any pile is the failure mode that gets firms in trouble. Sample, don't skip.

choices.label: Review every single high-confidence row by hand
choices.explain: Defeats the purpose; you've now done the same work as before plus an AI bill.

choices.label: Re-run the AI to see if the confidence changes
choices.explain: Confidence is calibrated, not random; re-running just gives you another opinion.

hi-IN.title: Old-school reconciliation ki memory
hi-IN.md:
Articleship ke pehle saal mein, mereko HSBC ka bank reconciliation milta tha — 22 pages ka statement, ledger ki 18 pages, sab tally karna haath se. Tick mark ka stationery khatam ho jaata tha.

Aaj — same kaam 90 minute mein, aur exception list zyada complete hoti hai jitna humne kabhi haath se kiya. Time saved is real. But discipline same: low confidence wala pile humein dekhna hi padta hai.

en.title: The tick-mark generation
en.md: Old reconciliation work was tick marks and a magnifying glass. New reconciliation work is confidence thresholds and a sample plan. The work is shorter; the discipline is identical.

blocks.md:
Second named move. The **human-in-the-loop tier** is where the CA actually adds value. It is the bottom 5 to 15 percent of matches — the ones the model couldn't confidently resolve, and the ones above the rupee-value threshold regardless of confidence.

Why include high-rupee items even when they're high-confidence? Because the cost of a wrong match scales with the rupee value. A wrong ₹3,200 categorisation is a rounding error. A wrong ₹2,40,000 categorisation is a disclosure event.

The human-in-the-loop tier is not a fallback for AI failure; it is the part of the workflow where a CA's judgment, training, and signature are intentionally put on the line. Done well, this tier captures every item where being wrong would matter, while leaving the boring 80-percent to AI.

coach.role: Partner, mid-tier Pune firm, 22 years in practice

intro: Reconciliation week. Eight clients, four staff, one me. Here are the calls I had to make on the phone yesterday.
Pick whether each is genuinely human-in-the-loop work or whether the AI should have handled it on its own.

scenarios.situation: A bank line for ₹2,40,000 NEFT to 'REPL IND' matches a ledger entry for 'Repl Industries Pvt Ltd' for ₹2,40,000 on the same date. Confidence 97.
scenarios.explain: Auto-accept zone. Sample as part of the high-confidence batch; do not review individually.

scenarios.situation: A bank credit of ₹47,00,000 from a party never seen before, narration 'INWARD REMITTANCE'. No ledger match. The amount is 12 percent of monthly turnover.
scenarios.explain: High rupee value, no match, possible regulatory implication (FEMA/source of funds). Stop the workflow, investigate, signoff before proceeding.

scenarios.situation: 847 small UPI payments under ₹500 each, all matching electricity-bill style narrations to 'Bescom payment' ledger heads. Confidence 96 across all.
scenarios.explain: Auto-accept; sample 30 of the 847; the rupee value per row is too low to demand individual review.

scenarios.situation: A ledger entry for ₹3,80,000 to 'Director Loan Repayment' with no corresponding bank debit in the period. Period-end mismatch.
scenarios.explain: Director-related party transaction with no bank evidence. Audit-sensitive; CA must investigate, classify, and sign.

scenarios.situation: Bank charges of ₹680 on the 19th, no ledger entry. Confidence 0 (no match).
scenarios.explain: AI flags the unmatched bank charges and proposes a journal entry. CA reviews the proposed entry as a batch with the other 12 unmatched bank charges. Within the AI workflow.

scenarios.situation: A bank credit for ₹14,28,000 matches a ledger entry for ₹14,82,000 for the same vendor on the same date. Confidence 72.
scenarios.explain: Same vendor, same date, ₹54,000 difference. Classic sign of a comma-displacement booking error or a partial payment. CA judgment required to determine which.

blocks.title: The classic trap: collapsing the tiers
blocks.md:
Under deadline pressure, every firm tries the same shortcut: "let's just review everything with confidence below 90 and accept the rest." Two months later you realise you've been auto-accepting matches above 90 with no sampling at all, and the high-rupee mismatches above 90 have been silently flowing through for a quarter.

**Sampling is not optional. Rupee-value thresholds are not optional. The two layers exist for a reason.** When you collapse them, you've stopped doing reconciliation; you've started doing wishful thinking.

blocks.prompt: You're starting an AI-assisted reconciliation engagement for a 47-outlet retail chain. Order these design decisions, first to last.

items.label: Define confidence thresholds (e.g., 70 / 95) for the engagement
items.detail: Set in writing in the engagement letter; revisit quarterly.

items.label: Define the rupee-value threshold for mandatory CA review regardless of confidence
items.detail: Single threshold in rupees; common starting point: ₹50,000 or 0.5% of monthly turnover.

items.label: Define the sampling plan for the auto-accept tier
items.detail: Sample size, sampling method (random or stratified), error tolerance.

items.label: Standardise input data — bank statement and ledger into common schema
items.detail: Date, amount, party, narration; one row per transaction.

items.label: Run the matcher and produce the scored match table
items.detail: Output: bank_line_id, ledger_line_id, score, top-3 alternates.

items.label: Apply the review tiers — sample auto, review medium, investigate low + high-rupee
items.detail: Single workflow with three queues.

items.label: Partner reviews exception list and signs off
items.detail: Working papers preserved with the eval log.

blocks.hint: The design comes before the run. Most firms get this backwards and bolt review tiers on later.

blocks.expected:
## Match scoring rule

Given a bank line and a ledger line, compute the score from 0 to 100:

1. **Amount match (50 points)**
   - Exact match: 50
   - Within ₹1: 48
   - Within ₹100: 30
   - Otherwise: 0 (and the match is rejected — no further scoring)

2. **Date proximity (20 points)**
   - Same date: 20
   - Within 1 day: 16
   - Within 3 days: 10
   - Within 7 days: 4
   - Beyond 7 days: 0

3. **Narration similarity (20 points)**
   - Embedding similarity 0.95+: 20
   - 0.85 to 0.95: 14
   - 0.70 to 0.85: 8
   - Below 0.70: 0

4. **Reference number / cheque number / UPI ID match (10 points)**
   - Exact match present on both sides: 10
   - Partial match (e.g. last 6 digits): 6
   - No reference present on either side: 5 (neutral; can't penalise the absence)
   - Reference present on one side, not the other: 0

Final score = sum of the four. Cap at 100.

**Notes**
- If amount match scores 0, do not produce a candidate at all.
- If amount, date, and reference all match exactly, score is at least 80 even without narration.
- Embedding-similarity threshold is calibrated against the client's own narration vocabulary; recompute every 6 months.

blocks.prompt: Which of these are valid reasons to escalate a match into the human-in-the-loop tier? (Select all that apply.)

choices.label: Confidence below the review threshold (e.g., under 70)
choices.explain: Right. Low-confidence matches need human eyes regardless of value.

choices.label: Rupee value above the engagement threshold even if confidence is high
choices.explain: Right. Wrong matches scale in cost with rupee value; high-value items always get human review.

choices.label: Counterparty appears for the first time in the period
choices.explain: Right. New counterparties — especially with significant amounts — warrant CA judgment for KYC and source-of-funds reasons.

choices.label: It's a Friday afternoon
choices.explain: Workflow design should be deterministic, not weather-dependent.

SaaS bhai phone karta hai — "sir, hamara tool fully automated bank reconciliation karta hai, koi human review ki zaroorat nahi."

Accha. Toh ₹14,28,000 jab ₹14,82,000 ho jaata hai, kaun signature karta hai working papers pe? Tool ke CEO toh client ke saamne kabhi nahi baithenge.

en.md: Any vendor selling 'fully automated' reconciliation is selling you full automation of the risk, not full automation of the work. The signature is still yours.

blocks.title: Field Notes: ₹47 Lakh Unmatched, ₹6 Lakh That Caught a Fraud
blocks.source: Audit senior at Patel Shroff & Co., engaged by a Surat textile exporter with ₹420 crore turnover
blocks.story:
The client — a fourth-generation cotton-and-rayon exporter operating across **3 banks, 11 current accounts, and 2 export-credit accounts** — handed over an FY24-25 bank-rec backlog that was, charitably, a nightmare. **₹47.3 lakh of unreconciled bank entries** across 12 months. The previous year's articleship team had given up in February and tagged everything as 'suspense — pending'. Audit clock ticking.

Patel Shroff piloted a confidence-scored matcher against 14,200 bank lines and 16,800 ledger lines. The output: **₹41.1 lakh auto-matched at confidence above 0.92** (vendor narration similarity, amount equality, date proximity within 3 days). **₹6.2 lakh in the review queue** — 187 items, sorted by confidence ascending, with the top 14 flagged for a high-rupee secondary review regardless of confidence.

The audit senior worked the queue in **4.5 hours**. Three patterns emerged in the bottom-confidence cluster: (1) round-number ₹50,000 transfers to a vendor named 'NEFT-RAJ ENT PVT LTD' that the model could not match to any ledger entry; (2) the same ₹50,000 amount appearing **17 times across 9 months**; (3) the recipient account, when the senior pulled the IFSC, traced to a relative of the client's payroll head.

**Embezzlement. ₹8.5 lakh over the FY, hidden in a 14,200-line bank statement, surfaced because the AI could not confidently match the entries and refused to silently assume.** The client's payroll head was let go; criminal complaint filed January 2026.

The partner, retelling the story at an ICAI study circle, kept saying the same line: *'The AI did not catch the fraud. The AI made the fraud catchable.'*
blocks.takeaway: Confidence scores are the point. A binary matcher would have force-matched those entries to something. The unmatched bottom 5% is where the value lives — for the auditor, and sometimes for the client.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Anand's First AI Reconciliation — Read the Confidence Scores
blocks.setup:
It is **Wednesday, 8 April 2026, 11:20 AM**. **Anand** is in week 8 of the rollout. The pilot bookkeeping is stable; **Sundari** has cleared him to run his first AI-assisted bank reconciliation on a real client — a Pune-based industrial cleaning supplies distributor with **₹64 crore turnover** and a single ICICI current account.

The matcher has finished its run on the March 2026 bank statement. **2,847 bank lines, 3,104 ledger lines.** The output is sitting on Anand's screen. **2,663 lines auto-matched at confidence above 0.90** (94%). **184 lines in the review queue** — the bottom 6%, sorted ascending.

Sundari is at her desk. *'Anand, your queue. Walk me through your interpretation. I will sit with you for the first one. After that you are on your own — but we both sign before it goes to the client.'*

coach.name: Senior-CA Sundari
coach.role: Senior CA, 9 years post-qualification, runs bookkeeping for the AI pilot cohort

stages.prompt: **Stage 1.** The top of the review queue — the lowest-confidence row. Bank line: *'NEFT-N-MNO LOGISTICS-INV982'*, ₹3,42,000, dated 14 March. Confidence: 0.41. Closest ledger candidate: 'M N O Logistics Pvt Ltd', ₹3,42,000, dated 17 March, invoice ref blank. What is your move?

options.label: Confidence is below 0.5, so reject the match outright and escalate to Sundari.
options.explain: You have skipped the diagnostic step. A 0.41 confidence does not mean the match is wrong; it means the model could not be sure. The amounts tie exactly, the names are clearly the same vendor, and the dates are 3 days apart — which is normal for end-of-month banking. Investigate before escalating.

options.label: The amounts tie, the vendor names match modulo formatting, and the dates are within a normal end-of-month window. Pull the underlying invoice (INV982 referenced in the narration), confirm the ledger entry is the same invoice, and accept the match with a manual override note in the eval log.
options.explain: **Correct.** Low confidence is a flag, not a verdict. The matcher could not be sure because it had no invoice number on the ledger side; you can be sure because you can open the invoice. Manual override with a note is exactly what the eval log exists to capture.

options.label: Force-accept the match. The amounts tie exactly; that is enough.
options.explain: Amount-only matching is the failure mode the AI was supposed to fix. ₹3,42,000 might be the round number for two different invoices to two different vendors. Verify the invoice reference in the narration before accepting.

options.label: Mark it 'unreconciled' and move on. The model could not match it, so you cannot.
options.explain: You have outsourced your judgment to the model. The CA's job in the review queue is precisely to do what the model cannot. If you replicate the model's uncertainty, the review tier adds zero value.

stages.prompt: **Stage 2.** Next row. Bank line: *'IMPS-SELF-TRF'*, ₹85,000, dated 22 March. Confidence: 0.18. Closest ledger candidate: 'Director's loan repayment', ₹85,000, dated 22 March. Sundari watches.

options.label: Same date, same amount, narration says 'self transfer', and the ledger entry is a director's loan repayment. Accept with override and add a note: 'Self-transfer narration consistent with director loan repayment per ledger; verified with bank statement and Mr. X's loan account.'
options.explain: **Yes.** The model's confidence was low because 'IMPS-SELF-TRF' is a generic narration that could be anything. You have specific knowledge — the director loan account exists, the amount matches, the date matches. Document the reasoning in the override note. This is exactly what classify-then-verify is for.

options.label: Reject — 'self-transfer' is too generic, the model is right to be uncertain.
options.explain: The model's uncertainty is about narration, not about the underlying transaction. You have additional context (the director loan ledger entry) the model did not have. Use it.

options.label: Accept silently without a note.
options.explain: Eval log entries with no override note become liabilities at audit time. Two years from now nobody will remember why this was overridden. 'Verified per ledger and bank statement' is 8 words and saves an entire audit defence.

options.label: Forward the entry to the client and ask them to confirm.
options.explain: Bouncing every low-confidence entry back to the client defeats the purpose of doing the reconciliation. The client hired you to resolve these, not to triage them back. Use the ledger evidence in front of you first; escalate to the client only if you cannot resolve internally.

stages.prompt: **Stage 3.** A pattern appears. You spot **6 entries** in the queue, all ₹49,000, all on consecutive Fridays, all with narration 'IMPS-PAYROLL-ADJ'. Confidence on each: 0.31. No matching ledger entries. The client's payroll head signs off on weekly payroll adjustments. What do you do?

options.label: Force-match each one to a payroll-adjustment line and move on. Six small entries, total ₹2.94 lakh, immaterial.
options.explain: Materiality is not just rupee value. A repeating pattern of round-number unmatched entries with the same narration is a fraud signal — the Surat textile case, almost line for line. ₹2.94 lakh today, ₹8 lakh by year-end if you ignore it.

options.label: Stop. Flag the cluster to Sundari before processing any of them. Pull the IFSC of the recipient account from the bank statement, cross-check against the vendor master, and check whether ₹49,000 sits just under any internal approval threshold.
options.explain: **This is the move.** Six round-number weekly transfers, no ledger backing, generic narration. The IFSC check, the vendor-master cross-check, and the threshold check are the three diagnostic steps. ₹49,000 just under a ₹50,000 threshold is a classic structuring tell. Sundari nods grimly — she has seen this before.

options.label: Open a 'suspense' account and park all six entries there. Resolve at year-end.
options.explain: Suspense accounts are where fraud goes to die — quietly, undetected, until the next auditor finds it. The whole reason the AI surfaced these in the review queue is so you would investigate them now, not bury them.

options.label: Ask the payroll head directly what the entries are.
options.explain: If the payroll head is the one structuring transfers under their own approval threshold, you have just told them you noticed. Bypass to Sundari and the partner first; client conversations come after the firm has formed a hypothesis.

stages.prompt: **Stage 4.** The queue is cleared. **165 items resolved with overrides; 14 escalated; 5 (including the payroll cluster) flagged for partner review.** What do you put in the eval log summary before signing off?

options.label: 'Reconciliation complete.'
options.explain: Two years from now this entry tells nobody anything. The eval log only protects you if it is informative. One sentence is not informative.

options.label: Summary noting: total lines, auto-match rate, review-queue size, count of manual overrides, count of escalations, count of flagged-for-partner items, hash of the matcher output, model version, and a one-paragraph note on the payroll cluster pattern with the IFSC and the rationale for partner escalation.
options.explain: **Comprehensive and queryable.** The numbers let any future reviewer reconstruct what happened; the payroll-cluster note ensures the pattern is not lost if the engagement changes hands. This is what an eval log entry should look like. Sundari approves.

options.label: Save a screenshot of the matcher output to the engagement folder.
options.explain: Screenshots are not searchable, not append-only, not standardised. The Surat exporter case relied on the firm being able to query 'show me every entry above ₹40,000 with confidence below 0.5 in the last 12 months'. Screenshots cannot answer that.

options.label: Email the summary to the partner.
options.explain: **Also correct, but as well as the eval log entry, not instead of.** The eval log is the durable record; the partner email is the workflow notification. Half-credit for email-only, full-credit for eval log entry plus partner notification.

outcomes.perfect: Sundari closes her notebook. *'Anand, this is what the rollout was supposed to look like. You did not just clear the queue — you read the queue. The payroll cluster goes to Pramod this evening.'* You used the confidence score as a triage tool, used your CA judgment in the review tier, spotted a fraud pattern in the bottom-confidence cluster, and logged the work properly. The Surat partner's line — 'the AI did not catch the fraud, the AI made the fraud catchable' — applies to your work today.
outcomes.good: Sundari is happy with most of the calls but corrects you on one or two. The mechanics are right; the discipline of the override note and the eval log entry needs another pass. Re-read the lesson on the human-in-the-loop tier and the difference between the model's uncertainty and yours.
outcomes.learn: Sundari is firm. *'Anand, a confidence score is information, not a verdict. The 6% in the queue is where the work is — not the 94% above the threshold. Re-read the lesson, especially the sections on confidence-scored matching and the human-in-the-loop tier. We will go through the queue together tomorrow.'* The fraud pattern in stage 3 is in the textbook for a reason. Do not miss it next time.

points: Reconciliation is fuzzy matching at scale; AI is a fuzzy matcher; the alignment is structural, not magical.
Confidence-scored matches are the only output worth shipping — binary match/no-match throws away the most useful information AI produces.
Three tiers: auto-accept with sampling, medium review row-by-row, low investigate fully. Plus a rupee-value override that promotes high-value matches regardless of confidence.
The human-in-the-loop tier is not a fallback; it is where the CA's judgment is intentionally placed — small in volume, decisive in impact.
Collapsing the tiers under deadline pressure is the failure mode every firm rediscovers; sampling and rupee thresholds are non-negotiable.

blocks.notesByline: Notes by Anand, articleship batch of 2024

blocks.md:
Two months ago, an articled assistant in a Hyderabad firm filed a GSTR-3B based on ChatGPT's summary of the input tax credit position. ChatGPT confidently cited "Notification 24/2023-Central Tax" as the basis for a partial reversal. The notification number existed; the content did not match. The firm received a notice three weeks later. The articled assistant's batchmates now refer to him, behind his back, as Section-Sixteen Sandeep.

This lesson exists so you do not become the next Sandeep. Indian tax law is the most complex, most-amended body of practical knowledge any working CA touches. AI can either be your fastest research assistant or your most confident liar. The difference is one design decision.

blocks.title: Mental model: tax laws are knowable; AI shouldn't guess
blocks.md:
Indian tax law is finite. Every notification, every circular, every section is published, dated, indexed. There is no good reason for an AI to *guess* a section number when the actual document is one retrieval away.

**If your AI workflow asks the model to remember a tax position, you have built it wrong. If it asks the model to read a specific provision and apply it, you have built it right.**

This is the boundary that separates real tax-AI work from press-release tax-AI work. Memory is unreliable; retrieval is auditable.

hi-IN.title: Section-Sixteen Sandeep ki kahaani
hi-IN.md:
Sandeep ne ChatGPT ko poocha — "Section 16 ke under ITC kya conditions hain?" ChatGPT ne paragraph likha. Sandeep ne copy kara, GSTR-3B mein ITC claim kar di.

Do hafte baad — notice. Reason: ChatGPT ne Rule 36(4) ka old version use kara tha, October 2022 wala. Current rule alag hai. ChatGPT ki training data 2024 ki thi par specific notification timeline confused tha.

Learning: jab tu RAG nahi karta, tu basically Wikipedia ki ek 2-saal purani print copy se filing kar raha hai.

en.title: The Sandeep cautionary tale
en.md: Sandeep filed a GSTR-3B based on a ChatGPT paragraph that quoted a superseded version of Rule 36(4). The notice arrived in three weeks. Without RAG against the current corpus, you're filing against a stale snapshot.

blocks.text: Move 1 — RAG against the actual GST/IT Act

blocks.md:
First named move. Build (or buy) a **RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline** indexed over the actual primary sources.

For an Indian tax practice, the corpus is roughly: the CGST Act, IGST Act, SGST Acts of relevant states, CGST Rules, CBIC notifications and circulars (last 5 years minimum), the Income Tax Act, Income Tax Rules, CBDT circulars, the major DTAAs your clients deal with, and selected case law from ITAT, High Courts, and Supreme Court.

The pipeline does this: when a question comes in, the system retrieves the relevant passages from the corpus, then asks the model to answer *based only on those passages*, with verbatim quotes and section citations.

The model is no longer recalling; it is reading. The difference is the difference between a notice and no notice.

blocks.title: What RAG looks like end-to-end for a single tax question

steps.label: Step 1 — The question arrives
steps.body: Client asks: 'Can we claim ITC on the new Mahindra Bolero we bought for our sales team?' Plain English, full of context the model needs.

steps.label: Step 2 — Retrieve
steps.body: The retriever scans the corpus and returns: Section 17(5)(a) CGST Act (the blocked-credit list), Circular 156/12/2021, the relevant ITAT decision on motor vehicles for sales staff, and any state-specific notification.

steps.label: Step 3 — Ground
steps.body: The retrieved passages are stuffed into the model's context with the instruction: 'Answer only based on these passages. Quote verbatim. If the passages do not address the question, say so.'

steps.label: Step 4 — Generate with citation
steps.body: Model returns: 'Section 17(5)(a) blocks ITC on motor vehicles for transportation of persons with seating capacity of 13 or fewer, except when used for further supply of such vehicles, transportation of passengers, or driving training. The Bolero, used for sales staff transport, falls within the blocked list. ITC is not available.' Cites Section 17(5)(a) verbatim and the circular.

steps.label: Step 5 — CA verifies
steps.body: You open Section 17(5)(a) on the CBIC site or your bare-act subscription, confirm the quote is exact, and confirm the conclusion. Two minutes; high signal.

steps.label: Step 6 — Eval log
steps.body: Question, retrieved passages, model response, your verification note, and your final advice all logged with timestamp and reviewer name. If a notice arrives in 2028, you can defend the position.

blocks.prompt: What is the most important property of a RAG-based tax answer?

choices.label: Every assertion is grounded in a retrieved passage that the CA can independently open and verify
choices.explain: Right. Verifiability is the entire point. Without it, RAG is just a slower direct LLM ask.

choices.label: It uses the most expensive model available
choices.explain: Model choice is secondary. A cheap model with good retrieval beats an expensive model that hallucinates.

choices.label: It returns the answer in under one second
choices.explain: Speed is irrelevant for tax research; correctness is the whole game.

choices.label: It uses a fashionable vector database
choices.explain: The DB is plumbing. The discipline matters.

hi-IN.title: RAG = bare-act ki digital body double
hi-IN.md:
Bare act humein hamesha bola gaya — "yahi sach hai, baaki sab opinion." RAG basically AI ke liye bare act ki digital body double hai.

Bina RAG ke AI woh senior CA hai jo conference mein sun ke aaya hai aur memory se quote kar raha hai. Theek hai shaayad. Galat ho toh defendable nahi.

RAG ke saath AI woh senior CA hai jo bare act khol ke baith ke padh raha hai. Theek hai aur defendable hai.

en.title: RAG as digital bare-act
en.md: Without RAG, the model is a senior CA quoting from memory at a conference. With RAG, the model is the same CA reading from the bare act with the page open. One is defensible; the other is folklore.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The never-ship rule for filings

blocks.md:
Second named move, and the most important rule in this entire course.

**The never-ship rule: AI never produces the version of a statutory filing that is filed.** Not GSTR-1, not GSTR-3B, not Form 26Q, not Form 3CD, not the income tax return, not the audit report. AI may draft. AI may populate. AI may cross-check. The version uploaded to the GST portal or the income tax e-filing portal is the version produced and reviewed by a human CA, signed under the CA's name and ICAI registration.

This is not a stylistic preference. The Chartered Accountants Act, the Income Tax Act, the GST law, and the relevant ICAI guidance notes all assume — explicitly — that statutory filings are the work product of the chartered accountant. Outsourcing the signature to an LLM is not a workflow innovation; it is a contravention.

In practice this means: every filing has a CA review step that meaningfully changes or confirms the AI draft. Rubber-stamping is not review.
