scenarios.explain: Crosses the line, twice. First: vendor cannot waive the CA's statutory liability with a cash guarantee. Second: filing without per-client review is professional misconduct, not innovation.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the rubber-stamp review
blocks.md:
The most common failure mode is not skipping review entirely; it is doing review badly. A senior who 'reviews' a GSTR-3B by clicking through it in 90 seconds and signing has not reviewed it.

The test is simple: **how many changes did the review produce?** If the answer is consistently zero, you are not reviewing; you are stamping. Either AI is producing a perfect output (extraordinarily unlikely), or you are missing things (overwhelmingly likely).

A review that doesn't change anything 90% of the time is a review that catches nothing 100% of the time.

blocks.instruction: Write the system prompt for a RAG-based GST advisory assistant. The corpus is indexed CGST/IGST Acts, CGST Rules, CBIC notifications and circulars (last 5 years). The assistant must refuse to answer questions outside the retrieved passages and must cite section + sub-section + clause for every position.
blocks.expected:
## System prompt — GST Advisory RAG

You are a GST advisory assistant for a chartered accountant practice in India. Your job is to answer questions about GST law strictly based on the retrieved passages provided in this conversation.

**Sourcing rules**
1. Every assertion you make MUST be supported by a retrieved passage. Quote the relevant clause verbatim, in quotation marks, before drawing the conclusion.
2. Cite section, sub-section, clause, and source document for every position. Format: 'Section 17(5)(a), CGST Act, 2017'. For circulars: 'Circular No. 156/12/2021-GST, dated 21 June 2021'. For notifications: 'Notification No. 22/2018-Central Tax, dated 14 September 2018'.
3. If the retrieved passages do not address the question, respond exactly: 'The retrieved corpus does not contain a passage that addresses this question. Please consult the bare act, the relevant circular, or a senior partner.' Do not attempt to answer from training data.
4. If you find a conflict between two retrieved passages (e.g., a notification superseded by a later one), surface the conflict and refuse to draw a conclusion until a CA resolves it.

**Output format**
- Begin with a one-sentence answer.
- Follow with the verbatim quote(s) from the retrieved passage(s).
- Follow with a 1 to 3 paragraph reasoned application of the quote to the facts of the question.
- End with a list of citations: section / sub-section / clause / document title / date.
- Add a 'For CA review' note flagging any open factual assumptions you made about the client (e.g., 'assumes the vehicle has 13 or fewer seats; verify').

**Forbidden**
- Do not paraphrase a section without quoting the underlying language first.
- Do not cite a section number you have not seen in the retrieved passages.
- Do not give a tax position with confidence above 'highly likely'; the final position is the CA's call.
- Do not generate the file that will be uploaded; you draft for human review only.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Section 16(2)(c) Interpretation That Did Not Exist
blocks.source: Tax partner at Rao Krishnan & Co., a Chennai CA firm with a strong GST advisory practice
blocks.story:
On 4 September 2025, a junior CA at the firm — newly qualified, four months in — used a general-purpose chat AI to draft the GSTR-3B for a logistics client with **₹74 crore turnover and a ₹38 lakh ITC mismatch** flagged by the GSTN portal. The mismatch was on inward supplies from a vendor whose GSTR-1 had not been filed for the period.

The junior asked the AI to draft an explanatory note for the client justifying the ITC claim. The AI obliged with a confident, fluent two-paragraph note citing **'the established CBIC interpretation of Section 16(2)(c) read with Rule 36(4), per Circular No. 183/15/2022-GST dated 27 December 2022, which clarifies that the recipient's ITC entitlement is preserved where the recipient has discharged its statutory obligations'**.

The interpretation did not exist. Circular 183/15/2022-GST exists, but it does not say what the AI claimed. The plain reading of Section 16(2)(c), reinforced by **multiple subsequent CBIC clarifications**, is the opposite — ITC is conditional on the supplier's tax actually reaching the government. The junior, trusting the citation looked specific (number, date, even a circular series), pasted the note into the client's working paper.

**The partner caught it on a 14-minute final review that evening.** She looked up the circular. The text bore no resemblance. *'If this had gone out under our letterhead and reached an ITAT bench, we would have spent the next 18 months explaining ourselves.'*

The firm's response was structural. Within 60 days, a **RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline** was built over the CGST Act, IGST Act, all CBIC circulars from 2017 onwards, and selected case law. **No AI tax output is now drafted without RAG retrieval, and every citation in any AI output must be verifiable against the retrieved source.** Junior CAs are trained, on day one, to copy any citation into the bare-act lookup before it leaves their screen.
blocks.takeaway: An LLM without RAG is a confident-sounding witness with no documents. A real CA practice cannot use it for tax work. The fix is not better prompting; it is a retrieval pipeline indexed on the bare act.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The AI-Drafted GST Notice Response — Spot the Fake Circular
blocks.setup:
It is **Friday, 1 May 2026, 3:30 PM**. **Anand** is in week 12 of the rollout. The pilot has expanded to GST advisory work. A long-standing client — a Pune auto-component manufacturer with **₹140 crore turnover** — has received a **DRC-01A intimation** from the GST department: alleged **₹22 lakh ITC excess claim** for FY24-25 on inputs procured from a vendor whose GSTR-1 was filed late.

Anand has used the firm's general-purpose chat AI (no RAG, against firm policy, but he is in a hurry) to draft a 2-page response. The draft is on his screen. **Partner Pramod** walks past, glances at it, and stops.

*'Anand. Read me the third paragraph.'*

The paragraph reads: *'The recipient's entitlement to ITC stands preserved per the principle laid down in **Circular No. 224/18/2024-GST dated 11 July 2024**, which clarifies that procedural lapses by the supplier do not, in themselves, defeat the substantive right of the recipient to claim ITC where the conditions of Section 16(2) are otherwise satisfied.'*

Pramod folds his arms. *'Walk me through how you wrote that. Stage by stage.'*

coach.name: Partner Pramod
coach.role: Senior partner, 22 years post-qualification, runs the audit and assurance practice

stages.prompt: **Stage 1.** Pramod's first question: *'Did you verify Circular No. 224/18/2024-GST exists?'* What is your honest answer — and what is your move now?

options.label: Yes, it sounds like a real CBIC circular series. The number format is correct. I am 90% sure it exists.
options.explain: 'Sounds like' and 'number format is correct' is exactly how the Rao Krishnan junior shipped a fake circular. The format being plausible is what the model is good at; the existence of the document is something only the bare-act source can confirm. 90% sure is 100% wrong if the 10% is real.

options.label: No. I will pull up the CBIC GST circulars page right now and search for circular 224/18/2024-GST. If it does not exist, the entire paragraph is fabricated and I rewrite from primary source.
options.explain: **Correct.** The verification step takes 90 seconds. The cost of skipping it is a notice response to the GST department citing a circular that does not exist. Pramod nods — this is the response he was hoping for.

options.label: I will ask the AI to confirm whether the circular exists.
options.explain: Asking the model that fabricated the citation to confirm the citation is a category error. The model has no way to know whether what it generated is real; it will confidently say yes. You need an independent source — the actual CBIC website, or a paid commentary database.

options.label: I will check with the senior junior who handled this client last quarter.
options.explain: Junior-CA tribal knowledge is not a primary source. The CBIC circulars page is. Use the bare act, not the bench grapevine.

stages.prompt: **Stage 2.** You check. The circular does not exist. The closest real circular (No. 183/15/2022-GST) addresses a related but different question. Pramod: *'Now diagnose. Why did this happen?'*

options.label: I used a bad prompt. I will rewrite it.
options.explain: Prompt rewriting will not fix this. Even a perfectly worded prompt to a model with no access to the CBIC corpus will hallucinate citations — because the model has no source to retrieve from. The fix is structural, not stylistic.

options.label: I used a general-purpose chat AI that has no live retrieval over CBIC sources. With no source corpus to cite from, the model fills the citation slot with statistically plausible numbers and dates. The fix is to use the firm's RAG pipeline that retrieves from the actual CGST Act, CBIC circulars, and case law before generating the response.
options.explain: **Exactly.** This is the correct diagnosis. A chat AI without RAG is recalling from training data and inventing the gaps. A RAG pipeline forces the model to cite only from retrieved passages, with verbatim quotes. Pramod almost smiles — almost.

options.label: The model was outdated. Newer model would not have done this.
options.explain: Newer models hallucinate too. They hallucinate more fluently. Model version is not the failure mode; the absence of a retrieval pipeline is.

options.label: The AI is unreliable for tax work. We should stop using it.
options.explain: Throwing out AI is throwing out the baby with the bathwater. AI with RAG, with verbatim quoting, with mandatory CA review, is genuinely useful. AI without those things is dangerous. Distinguish the tool from its setup.

stages.prompt: **Stage 3.** Pramod nods. *'Now rewrite the response using the RAG pipeline. What do you instruct it to do, specifically, to prevent this happening again?'*

options.label: *'Draft a response to the DRC-01A intimation.'*
options.explain: Same vague prompt as before, just pointed at a different model. You have not added the structural guardrails. The RAG pipeline by itself does not enforce verbatim quoting; the prompt has to demand it.

options.label: Prompt: *'Draft a DRC-01A response based ONLY on the retrieved passages provided in this context. For every legal position taken, quote the relevant section, sub-section, or circular text verbatim in quotation marks before applying it. Cite each source as "Section X(Y)(Z), CGST Act, 2017" or "Circular No. NNN/MM/YYYY-GST dated DD Month YYYY". If the retrieved passages do not address a question, return the literal string "INSUFFICIENT CORPUS — escalate to CA" instead of attempting to answer.'*
options.explain: **This is the move.** Verbatim-quote requirement, structured citation format, and a loud-failure mode when the corpus is silent. Pramod recognises the discipline — it is the same rigour he was trained to apply to opinion notes 22 years ago. Now you have applied it to AI.

options.label: Prompt: *'Draft a DRC-01A response. Do not hallucinate.'*
options.explain: Telling a model 'do not hallucinate' has been studied extensively and does not work. Mechanism beats instruction. RAG plus verbatim-quote requirement plus loud-failure mode is mechanism.

options.label: Prompt: *'Draft a response and add citations.'*
options.explain: 'Add citations' is exactly what got you the fake circular. The model added citations, just not real ones. The improvement is forcing the citation to come from the retrieved passage, not from the model's training data.

stages.prompt: **Stage 4.** Pramod's last question, the one that decides this lesson: *'The RAG-drafted response is ready. The client wants to file the DRC-01A response by Monday. Who signs?'*

options.label: The AI drafted it, you reviewed it, you sign as the prepare-er. The client signs as the assessee. We file Monday.
options.explain: An articled assistant cannot sign a tax response that goes to the GST department under the firm's name. The CA who signs is a qualified CA whose name and ICAI number appear on the engagement. The AI drafts; the junior reviews; the senior CA signs, full stop.

options.label: The AI drafted it. I reviewed it and verified every citation. Sundari did substantive review. You sign as the partner. The eval log entry captures every step. We file Monday.
options.explain: **This is the correct chain.** AI is a tool, not a signatory. Junior verifies citations against the bare act. Senior reviews the substance. Partner signs. Every step in the eval log. This is the never-ship rule applied correctly: AI never produces the version that is filed.

options.label: The AI signs digitally — this is the future of practice, partner.
options.explain: AI has no ICAI registration. AI cannot be disciplined by the institute. AI cannot be sued by the client. AI cannot sign. This is not a debate about future-of-practice; it is a current-law fact.

options.label: Skip the partner signature this once — we are short on time, the response is straightforward, and the eval log will document everything.
options.explain: An eval log records what happened; it does not authorise what should not have happened. The partner signature is the four-eye review's whole point. 'We were in a hurry' is the opening line of every ICAI inquiry transcript.

outcomes.perfect: Pramod uncrosses his arms. *'Anand, you got there. Verify the circular, diagnose the failure as architectural not prompt-level, rebuild on RAG with verbatim-quote discipline, and never confuse drafting with signing. Now go redraft. We file Monday under my signature, with your prep work and Sundari's review in the eval log.'* You have understood the most important rule in the entire course: AI never produces the version of a statutory filing that is filed.
outcomes.good: Pramod is satisfied that you can recover but corrects you on the prompt design or the signing chain. Re-read the lesson, especially the never-ship rule and the structure of a RAG prompt. Bring the redraft on Saturday morning.
outcomes.learn: Pramod is patient. *'Anand, this is the lesson. AI without RAG hallucinates citations. AI with RAG drafts; the CA signs. Re-read the lesson — the RAG move and the never-ship rule. The Rao Krishnan story is in the textbook because someone almost destroyed a 30-year practice on a Friday afternoon. Do not let that be us.'* The DRC-01A response gets redrafted on Saturday. Together.

points: Indian tax law is finite and indexed; there is no excuse for asking AI to recall when retrieval is one query away.
RAG against the actual GST/IT acts, rules, circulars, and case law turns the model from a hallucinator into a reader.
The never-ship rule: AI never produces the version of a statutory filing that is filed; the CA does, after substantive review.
Substantive review is measured by changes made; a review that catches nothing is not a review.
Every citation is verified against the source by a human whose name is in the eval log; no exceptions, no shortcuts.

Three years from now, a notice will arrive at a firm that used AI for an engagement in 2026. The Assessing Officer or the ICAI inspector will ask: "Show me how this position was reached. Who reviewed what. What did the model produce. What did the human change. What model was used. When."

If the firm can answer those questions in fifteen minutes from a structured log, the engagement is defensible. If it cannot, it doesn't matter how good the original work was; the firm is defending itself with a story instead of a record.

This lesson is about building that record. It is the least exciting topic in the entire course and quite possibly the most important.

blocks.title: Mental model: AI assists, the CA signs
blocks.md:
There is exactly one role AI plays in a regulated accounting practice: **assistant**. The signature, the opinion, the responsibility, and the liability live with the CA. Always. Without exception.

The audit trail is the evidence of this division of labour. It captures, for every AI-assisted output, what the model produced, what the human changed, who approved the change, and when. If a regulator, a partner, or a future court wants to know how a number was reached, the audit trail is the answer.

**No audit trail, no defensible engagement.** It really is that binary.

Aaj — eval log JSON mein hai. Searchable, timestamped, hash-verified. Audit ke time 15 minute mein nikaal sakte ho. Kaam wahi hai — paper kam hai, discipline same hai. Jisko discipline lagta hai useless overhead, woh first notice mein samjhega working papers ka asli matlab kya hai.

en.md: Old working papers were tick marks and partner initials in a manila file. New working papers are timestamped JSON in an eval log. The format is digital; the discipline is identical.

blocks.md:
First named move. The **eval log** is a structured, append-only record of every meaningful AI interaction in your firm.

For each entry: the engagement ID, the date and timestamp, the model and version, the exact prompt sent (or its hash if the prompt is templated), the documents retrieved into context, the response received, who reviewed it, what they changed, and the final artefact ID it contributed to.

This is not a feature to be added later. It is the precondition for using AI in regulated work at all. A firm that uses AI without an eval log is a firm that has decided, possibly without realising it, to defend itself with anecdotes.

The practical setup is unglamorous: a database table, a few middleware lines that log every API call, and a retention policy that matches your audit retention (typically 7 years in India for tax records, 8 for company records under the Companies Act).

blocks.title: What it looks like to defend an AI-assisted position from 2026 in 2028

steps.label: Step 1 — The notice arrives
steps.body: October 2028: an Assessing Officer questions the ITC claim of ₹4.7 lakh on motor vehicles for sales staff in your client's FY 2025-26 GSTR-3B. The position was that the vehicles fell within the 'driver training' exception. Why?

steps.label: Step 2 — Pull the eval log entries
steps.body: Search engagement_id ABC-26-Q4-GST for any entry tagged 'motor_vehicle_itc'. You find 4 entries, dating Oct 2026 to Mar 2027.

steps.label: Step 3 — Reconstruct the position
steps.body: Each entry shows the prompt, retrieved passages (Sec 17(5)(a), Circular 156/12/2021, an ITAT Mumbai 2024 decision), the model's draft conclusion, the reviewer (Anand, 14-Oct-2026), changes made (2 substantive corrections), partner approval (Vidya, same day), and the final advisory note ID.

steps.label: Step 4 — Open the actual artefact
steps.body: From the entry, retrieve the final advisory note. The note cites the same passages, applies them to the client's specific facts (vehicles used 70% for sales-staff transport, 30% for driver training), and concludes with the partial-claim position.

steps.label: Step 5 — Defend or concede
steps.body: If the position is sound and the trail is clean, you have a defensible case file in the AO's hands within a week. If the position was weak, you concede early, pay, and learn — but you can defend the *process* even when conceding the substance.

steps.label: Step 6 — Without the eval log
steps.body: No eval log: 'Honestly Sir, I think the senior CA at the time looked at the relevant section and decided. Do we have it in writing? Let me check.' That is how engagement letters become disciplinary complaints.

blocks.prompt: Which of these belong in an eval log entry? (Select all that apply.)

choices.label: The exact prompt or a hash plus the prompt template version
choices.explain: Right. Without the prompt, you cannot reproduce the response or argue what was asked.

choices.label: The model name and version used
choices.explain: Right. Different model versions produce different outputs; defending an answer requires knowing which model produced it.

choices.label: The reviewer's identity and timestamp
choices.explain: Right. The audit trail must trace human responsibility.

choices.label: Marketing copy describing how impressive the AI workflow is
choices.explain: Brochure material has no place in working papers.

hi-IN.md:
Tea break pe partner pucheega — "abhi jo Q3 wala ITC position liya tha, kis basis pe?"

Bina eval log: "sir, articled assistant ne batayi thi, AI ne bhi same kaha tha, mereko sahi laga."  
With eval log: laptop khol, search 'ITC motor vehicle Q3', 14 second mein full trail dikha do.

Dono mein difference partner ki nazar mein partner ke level ka hi banta hai.

en.title: The chai-break test
en.md: If a partner can ask 'show me how we got to that position' and you can produce a full trail in 30 seconds, you have a real audit trail. If you have to start a sentence with 'I think,' you don't.

blocks.md:
Second named move. **Four-eye review** means every artefact that leaves the firm has been reviewed by at least two distinct chartered accountants — typically a senior who does substantive review and a partner who confirms the position and signs.

Four-eye review predates AI by decades. What changes with AI is the *target* of the review: the reviewer is not just checking the junior's work; they are checking the AI's draft *and* the junior's modifications *and* the underlying basis. Three things to verify, not one.

In practice, the review is a structured walk-through: open the eval log entry, read the prompt and retrieved passages, read the model's draft, read the changes the first reviewer made and why, then form an independent judgment on the final position. If the senior CA agrees, they sign. If not, they push back, the cycle repeats.

Four-eye review is non-negotiable for any artefact that goes out under the firm's name on a tax-relevant or audit-relevant matter.

intro: Final scenarios. These are the ones I see partners get wrong most often, and the ones the ICAI inspector will care about most.
For each, decide whether the audit-trail discipline holds or fails.

scenarios.situation: Every AI prompt and response is logged with timestamp, model version, and reviewer identity. Two CAs review every advisory before it ships.
scenarios.explain: Holds. Eval log + four-eye review = textbook discipline.

scenarios.situation: Prompts are logged but only the senior CA reviews. The partner signs based on the senior's verbal summary.
scenarios.explain: Fails. Partner signature without independent review collapses the four-eye discipline. The signature is on a document the partner did not actually examine.

scenarios.situation: AI is used heavily but no logs are kept; the firm relies on the partner's memory and the staff's working notes.
scenarios.explain: Fails badly. Memory and working notes are not an audit trail. First notice exposes the gap.

scenarios.situation: Logs are kept but stored in an individual staff member's personal laptop with no backup or retention policy.
scenarios.explain: Fails. Logs that cannot be retrieved 7 years later are no logs at all. Centralised storage with retention policy is required.

scenarios.situation: Eval log captures everything but reviewers regularly approve drafts in under 60 seconds with zero changes recorded across 47 consecutive engagements.
scenarios.explain: Fails. Statistical signature of rubber-stamping. A reviewer who never finds anything wrong is not reviewing. The pattern itself is a finding.

scenarios.situation: Every advisory note carries a footer: 'Drafted with AI assistance under [model and version]; reviewed by [name 1] on [date]; signed by [name 2, partner].' Filed alongside the eval log entry.
scenarios.explain: Holds. Disclosure to the client is good practice; the footer is the public-facing equivalent of the eval log entry.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the lone-reviewer shortcut
blocks.md:
Under deadline pressure, the four-eye review collapses into a one-eye review. The senior approves; the partner signs based on a verbal summary; the audit trail records two reviewers but only one actually looked.

**The discipline must survive March 31st.** A discipline that holds in October and breaks in March is not a discipline; it is a preference. Build the workflow so that the partner physically cannot sign without opening the artefact, and the eval log captures the time spent on review, not just the timestamp of the click.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Form 3CD That Almost Was Not Reviewed
blocks.source: ICAI disciplinary committee proceedings (anonymised), referencing a Western India CA firm
blocks.story:
The firm — three partners, 22 staff, a healthy mid-tier practice in a Tier-2 city — had been quietly using a chat AI to populate the **Form 3CD tax audit report** for FY23-24 engagements. The workflow, as the firm later told the inquiry, was: junior pastes the trial balance, AI populates the Form 3CD clauses, junior copies the AI output into the e-filing utility, senior 'looks at it', partner signs.

For one client — a **₹47 crore turnover** edible oils trader — the workflow ran on a Saturday evening on **27 January 2025**. The senior, on a personal call, did not look at the output. The partner, trusting the senior, signed without re-reviewing. The Form 3CD was filed on 28 January.

The filed form contained a **Clause 21(d) entry stating ₹0 for amounts disallowable under Section 40A(3)** (cash payments above the threshold). The actual ledger contained **17 cash payments above ₹10,000** for transport, totalling **₹4.83 lakh** that should have been reflected. The AI had not flagged them because it had been given only the GL summary, not the cash payments register.

A differential analysis by the GST department six months later cross-referenced the cash withdrawals against the disallowance disclosure. **Notice. Inquiry. ICAI complaint against the signing partner.**

The firm narrowly avoided action — the disciplinary committee accepted the partner's plea that the omission was inadvertent, fined the firm, and let the partner off with a censure. The committee's written observation, paraphrased: *'Where AI tooling is used in the preparation of statutory filings, the responsibility for review and sign-off remains, in every respect, with the chartered accountant. A workflow that does not contemplate substantive senior review of AI output is a workflow that does not meet professional standards.'*

The firm has since rebuilt its workflow. **Four-eye review is now mandatory; the eval log is auto-attached to every Form 3CD; no AI-touched filing leaves without two CA signatures.** The senior who skipped the review left the firm in May 2025.
blocks.takeaway: AI cannot sign Form 3CD — full stop. The signature is the chartered accountant's, the responsibility is the chartered accountant's, and the four-eye review is the only thing standing between you and an ICAI inquiry.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Design the 4-Eye AI Audit Trail Pramod Will Sign Off On
blocks.setup:
It is **Friday, 8 May 2026, 4:00 PM**. **Anand** is in the final week of the 90-day rollout. The pilot has worked. The numbers are good — bookkeeping margin is up 22%, reconciliation cycle time is down 38%, GST advisory turn-around is down 31%.

**Partner Pramod** has called Anand into his office. The window is open; Pune monsoon is one weekend away.

*'Anand. The pilot is over. We are taking AI firm-wide on Monday. Before we do, I want you to design the four-eye audit trail. What does AI do, what stays human, what does the eval log capture, and — this is the only question that actually matters — what would the ICAI accept if they came in here in 2028 and asked us to defend an AI-assisted Form 3CD from this year? Take me through it. Last battle.'*

coach.name: Partner Pramod
coach.role: Senior partner, 22 years post-qualification, runs the audit and assurance practice

stages.prompt: **Stage 1.** *'First. Draw the line. What does AI do, and what stays human, in a typical statutory engagement?'*

options.label: AI does everything procedural — bookkeeping, reconciliation, GST drafting, Form 3CD population, and final filing. CA reviews exceptions only.
options.explain: Two problems. First, AI cannot file — that is the never-ship rule. Second, exception-only review means systematic errors that look confident slip through unreviewed. The line between AI and CA is not 'exceptions vs everything', it is 'wide-and-fast vs narrow-and-deep'.

options.label: AI does the wide-and-fast first pass: categorisation, matching, extraction, drafting. CA does the narrow-and-deep review: confidence-stratified sampling on routine work, 100% review on statutory filings, and exclusive sign-off authority on anything filed under the firm's name.
options.explain: **Correct.** This is the classify-then-verify model applied at the engagement level. AI compresses volume; CA exercises judgment. Filings stay 100% with humans, no exceptions. Pramod nods.

options.label: AI is a junior. Treat its output exactly like a first-year articleship's output — review the same way, sign the same way.
options.explain: **Also a useful framing.** A first-year's work gets read by a senior, then by a partner, then signed. AI deserves at least the same scrutiny — arguably more, because AI's mistakes are confident-looking and patterned, not nervous and obvious. Half-credit alone, full-credit if you also gave the wide-and-fast vs narrow-and-deep answer.

options.label: AI advises the client directly via chat. CA reviews the chat log monthly.
options.explain: AI advising the client directly is the firm's professional indemnity going up in smoke. Clients get advice from CAs, not from chatbots wearing the firm's logo. Monthly review is post-hoc damage assessment, not professional service.

stages.prompt: **Stage 2.** *'Now the eval log. What does it capture? Be specific — I want to know what is in the table and what is not.'*

options.label: The eval log captures whether AI was used or not, yes/no, per engagement.
options.explain: A yes/no flag tells nobody anything in 2028. The defence value of an eval log is the granularity. 'Yes, we used AI on this engagement' is not a defence; 'here is the prompt, the retrieved context, the model version, the response, the changes made, the reviewer, the timestamp' is.

options.label: Per AI interaction: engagement ID, date and timestamp, model name and version, the exact prompt (or hash of templated prompt plus parameter values), the documents and passages retrieved into context, the full response, the reviewer ID, the changes made (diff or notes), the final artefact ID this contributed to. Append-only. Retained 7 years (tax) or 8 years (companies). No editing of historical entries.
options.explain: **Comprehensive.** Every field you would need to reconstruct a 2026 AI interaction in 2028. Append-only is non-negotiable; if entries can be edited, the log has zero defence value. Pramod is taking notes — literal notes.

options.label: Just the prompts. Responses are too long to store.
options.explain: Storing prompts without responses is like keeping the questions to an exam without the answers — uninvestigatable. Storage is cheap; defence is expensive. Store both.

options.label: A monthly summary spreadsheet that the partner reviews.
options.explain: Aggregate spreadsheets cannot answer specific questions like 'what did the AI propose for Clause 21(d) on this client's Form 3CD on 28 January 2025'. The eval log has to be queryable at the interaction level, not the month level.

stages.prompt: **Stage 3.** *'Four-eye review. What does it actually look like for an AI-assisted Form 3CD?'*

options.label: Senior reads the AI draft and clicks approve. Partner signs.
options.explain: This is the workflow that almost destroyed the firm in the disciplinary case. 'Reading and clicking approve' is not substantive review. The senior has to actually open the underlying ledger, the cash payments register, the related-party schedule, and form an independent view on whether the AI populated each clause correctly.

options.label: Senior opens the eval log entry, reads the prompt and the retrieved data, reads the AI's clause-by-clause population, opens the underlying source documents (cash register, party ledger, fixed-asset register, etc.) and independently verifies each material clause. Documents the review with notes per clause. Partner then independently re-verifies the high-risk clauses (40A(3), related-party transactions, ICDS adjustments, anything where the firm has had past notices) and signs.
options.explain: **This is what review actually means.** Two CAs, two independent walks through the source documents, two layers of judgment, eval log entry per material clause. The 17 cash payments in the disciplinary case would not have survived 30 seconds of this workflow.

options.label: AI does the review — a second model verifies the first model's output. CA signs.
options.explain: Two AI models that share training data share blind spots. 'AI cross-checking AI' is not a four-eye review; it is a single-eye review with extra steps. The four eyes have to be human.

options.label: Senior reviews everything. Partner signs without re-reviewing — the senior is qualified, after all.
options.explain: The four-eye review is two independent qualified eyes on the same artefact. If the partner signs without re-reviewing, you have a one-eye workflow with a partner stamp at the end. The disciplinary case is exactly this failure mode.

stages.prompt: **Stage 4.** *'Final question. ICAI walks in tomorrow and asks us to defend an AI-assisted Form 3CD we filed in this rollout. What is your one-page defence?'*

options.label: AI is a tool, the CA reviewed it, and the CA signed it. End of story.
options.explain: True in spirit, useless as a defence. The disciplinary committee will ask 'show us the review evidence'. 'The CA reviewed it' without artefacts is the same as 'we did the work, trust us'. Defence has to be evidentiary.

options.label: Pull the eval log entries for the engagement: every AI interaction, every prompt, every retrieved passage, every response, every reviewer's notes, every change made, every signature. Show the workflow document that defines the four-eye review and the never-ship rule. Show the partner's clause-by-clause review notes. Show the source document references. The defence is not a story; it is a stack of artefacts.
options.explain: **This is the defence.** Evidence beats narrative. The eval log plus the workflow definition plus the review notes is the documentary trail any disciplinary committee will accept. The disciplinary case in the textbook turned on the absence of exactly this — and the firm narrowly survived. Pramod looks satisfied.

options.label: Argue that AI is too new for the existing standards to apply.
options.explain: The Chartered Accountants Act, the Income Tax Act, and the ICAI guidance notes are technology-agnostic. They assume the CA is responsible. 'AI is too new' is not a recognised defence under any Indian professional standard. Do not even try.

options.label: Show the AI vendor's certifications and security audits.
options.explain: The vendor's certifications are not the firm's defence. The firm signed the Form 3CD under the firm's ICAI registration. The vendor has no ICAI registration. The defence has to be the firm's review and sign-off discipline, evidenced by the firm's eval log.

outcomes.perfect: Pramod stands up. *'Anand, you have just designed our firm-wide AI policy. Write it up over the weekend. We roll it out Monday with you co-presenting alongside me. The articleship clock has 14 months left on it; by the time you qualify, you will have done more for this firm than I did in my first 5 years post-qualification.'* You have internalised the single most important principle in the entire course: AI assists, the chartered accountant signs. The four-eye review is non-negotiable. The eval log is the precondition. The never-ship rule is law.
outcomes.good: Pramod is happy with the broad design but corrects you on the eval log granularity or the four-eye review structure. Re-read the lesson on the eval log and the lone-reviewer shortcut. Bring v2 of the policy on Monday morning.
outcomes.learn: Pramod is firm. *'Anand, this is the lesson the entire 90 days has been preparing you for. AI cannot sign. The CA signs, with evidence. Re-read the lesson on the eval log and the four-eye review. We will write the policy together on Monday.'* The disciplinary case in the field notes is in the textbook because a partner almost lost his ICAI registration over a Saturday-evening shortcut. Do not be that partner in 12 years.

points: AI assists; the CA signs. There is no other arrangement that survives a notice or an inspection.
The eval log is the precondition for using AI in regulated work — without it, you are defending yourself with anecdotes.
Four-eye review is non-negotiable for any artefact that ships under the firm's name; the AI changes what the eyes look at, not whether two pairs are required.
Substantive review produces changes; a reviewer who consistently makes zero changes is the statistical signature of rubber-stamping, and an inspector will catch the pattern.
Disclosure to the client of AI assistance is not legal advice; it is professional practice in 2026, and it earns more trust than it loses.

blocks.prompt: Sketch the eval log schema your firm would adopt next quarter. What fields do you absolutely need, what would be nice to have, and what is the policy for retention, access, and tamper-evidence? Imagine you are explaining the design to your senior partner, who is sceptical about adding 'more software' to the firm.

assessment.title: AI for Accounting Assessment
assessment.description: Tests judgment under realistic Indian accounting scenarios: when to use AI, when to verify, when to refuse. Mix of single and multi-select questions covering reconciliation, GST, TDS, audit trail discipline, and the line a CA cannot let AI cross.

questions.stem: Your articled assistant feeds 4,200 vendor invoices to ChatGPT and asks it to extract the GSTIN, taxable value, and IGST amount as a CSV. The output looks clean. Before you trust a single row of it, what is the **first** check you run?
questions.explanation: LLMs hallucinate numbers silently. The cheapest, fastest sanity check is to verify totals against the source. A 0.3 percent mismatch on 4,200 invoices is twelve wrong rows; a 5 percent mismatch is 210.

choices.label: Sum the taxable value column from the CSV and reconcile with the source-document total
choices.explanation: Right. Numbers are not text; if the totals do not match, no other check matters. This is the cheapest, highest-signal check you can run.

choices.label: Spot-check 10 random invoices for GSTIN format
choices.explanation: Useful, but secondary. A correctly formatted GSTIN with the wrong taxable value is still wrong; you catch that only with totals.

choices.label: Re-run the same prompt and see if the answer is identical
choices.explanation: LLMs are non-deterministic at temperature > 0; identical answers prove nothing about correctness, only about the seed.

choices.label: Trust it — the output looks well-formatted
choices.explanation: Formatted output is the easiest thing for an LLM to produce. Correct numbers are the hardest. Never confuse the two.

questions.stem: Which of these tasks belong on the AI side of the 80/20 split for an Indian CA practice? **Select all that apply.**
questions.explanation: AI shines at extraction, classification, and pattern-matching at scale. It must not own the signature on a statutory filing or judgment about whether a transaction qualifies for ITC under disputed jurisprudence.

choices.label: Drafting a first-pass classification of 6,000 expense entries into ledger heads
choices.explanation: Classic pattern-matching at scale; AI is excellent here, with a CA reviewing the long-tail and edge cases.

choices.label: Signing the audit report under Section 143 of the Companies Act
choices.explanation: A statutory signature is a CA's personal liability. AI cannot sign. Ever.

choices.label: Extracting GSTINs and invoice numbers from 800 PDF purchase bills
choices.explanation: OCR plus extraction is exactly where AI wins; verify totals, then proceed.

choices.label: Deciding whether a litigation provision should be disclosed in financial statements
choices.explanation: Disclosure judgment depends on materiality, management representations, and professional skepticism — none of which AI can carry.

questions.stem: An SME client in Surat asks: "Can you use AI to reconcile our GSTR-2A with the purchase register for FY 2025-26?" What is the right scoping answer?
questions.explanation: The right answer scopes AI to extraction and matching, keeps the CA on judgment, and names the deliverable. Anything that promises 'AI will reconcile' without a human review tier is reckless.

choices.label: Yes — AI will produce confidence-scored matches; matches above 95 percent we accept after sampling, between 70 and 95 we review row-by-row, below 70 we treat as unmatched and investigate
choices.explanation: Right. Tiered review by confidence is the only defensible workflow. The deliverable is matches plus exception list, not a finished reconciliation.

choices.label: Yes — we'll feed both files to ChatGPT and send you the output by Friday
choices.explanation: No version control, no confidence tiers, no audit trail. This is how firms get into trouble.

choices.label: No — AI cannot do reconciliations
choices.explanation: Wrong in the other direction. Reconciliation is exactly the kind of fuzzy matching where AI shines, given guardrails.

choices.label: Yes — but only if the client signs an indemnity
choices.explanation: Indemnity does not transfer professional responsibility for a statutory function. The defence is process, not paperwork.

questions.stem: You ask Claude: 'What is the TDS rate for a payment to a non-resident for technical services in May 2026?' It answers '10 percent under Section 195.' What is wrong with using that answer in client work?
questions.explanation: Section 195 rates depend on the nature of payment, treaty position, PAN availability, surcharge, and cess. A single number with no citation is a hallucination risk regardless of whether the number happens to be right.

choices.label: It is a single number with no citation to the actual section, treaty, or notification — and the answer depends on facts the model did not ask for
choices.explanation: Exactly. The right move is RAG against the actual Income Tax Act and treaty text, with the model citing the source you can verify.

choices.label: Nothing — Section 195 rates are well-known, the model is reliable here
choices.explanation: Section 195 rates depend on PAN, treaty, nature of services, surcharge, and cess. The number 10 may be wrong before you finish reading this.

choices.label: Claude is not a tax tool; you should only use ChatGPT
choices.explanation: Tool brand is irrelevant. The discipline — citation, verification, never-ship — is what matters.

choices.label: The model used 'percent' instead of '%'
choices.explanation: Cosmetic.

questions.stem: Your firm is building an internal AI tool to draft income tax computations. Which of the following are non-negotiable design requirements? **Select all that apply.**
questions.explanation: Audit trail, eval log, and human signoff are the floor. Cost optimisation matters but never at the expense of these.

choices.label: Every prompt + response is logged with timestamp, model version, and the documents in context
choices.explanation: If you cannot reproduce the AI's reasoning later, you cannot defend it. This is the audit trail.

choices.label: A CA must approve every computation before it leaves the firm
choices.explanation: Four-eye review is the floor for anything that goes to a client or the department.

choices.label: The tool must be the cheapest model available
choices.explanation: Cost matters but is not a non-negotiable. Quality and verifiability come first.

choices.label: Output must be in Excel format
choices.explanation: Format is a preference, not a discipline.

questions.stem: A junior tells you: 'I asked ChatGPT to find the section number for the GST rate on solar panels and it said Notification 24/2023. I checked the CBIC site — that notification is about cement.' What is the named pattern at work?
questions.explanation: This is a hallucination — the model produced a plausible-sounding but fabricated citation. The pattern has a name precisely because it is so common: never trust a citation you have not opened.

choices.label: Hallucination — a fabricated but plausible citation; the named rule is 'never trust a citation you have not opened'
choices.explanation: Yes. The fix is RAG, not faith. If the model can cite a real document and quote from it, you can verify; otherwise, treat every section number as a guess.

choices.label: Outdated training data
choices.explanation: It might also be outdated, but the deeper issue is fabrication: the model invented a connection that does not exist. Outdated would be a real notification with a wrong rate.

choices.label: User error in prompting
choices.explanation: The prompt was reasonable. The model's behaviour is the issue.

choices.label: GPU temperature drift
choices.explanation: Not a thing.

questions.stem: What does the 'classify-then-verify' move look like for a 14,000-line bank statement?
questions.explanation: AI proposes a category for each line; the CA's review is concentrated on flagged-low-confidence and high-rupee lines. The verify step is mandatory, not optional.

choices.label: AI assigns a ledger head and confidence score to each line; you sample high-confidence rows and review every low-confidence and every high-amount row
choices.explanation: Right. You concentrate human attention where it changes the answer.

choices.label: AI assigns a ledger head; you accept the output and move on
choices.explanation: This is exactly the failure mode the move is designed to prevent.

choices.label: You categorise everything by hand and use AI to check your work
choices.explanation: Backwards. You wasted the AI's strength on the part it was supposed to handle.

choices.label: You ask AI to design a categorisation scheme, then ignore the data
choices.explanation: Now you have neither the categorisation nor the data.

questions.stem: Your client's GSTR-2A and purchase register show a 6.4 percent mismatch on ITC for the quarter. Which of the following are reasonable AI-assisted next steps? **Select all that apply.**
questions.explanation: AI helps you triage the mismatch faster but cannot decide whether to claim disputed ITC. That decision is a CA's call.

choices.label: Use AI to bucket mismatches by reason — missing in 2A, value mismatch, GSTIN mismatch, period mismatch
choices.explanation: Bucketing is pure pattern-matching at scale. AI is excellent.

choices.label: Use AI to draft follow-up emails to vendors whose invoices are missing in 2A
choices.explanation: First-pass communication drafts are a great AI use case; CA reviews, then sends.

choices.label: Let AI decide which disputed ITC entries to claim
choices.explanation: ITC eligibility under Section 16 is a judgment call with audit risk. CA only.

choices.label: Submit the GSTR-3B based on AI's reconciliation without further review
choices.explanation: Filing is the never-ship line. Do not cross it.

questions.stem: A partner at your firm asks: 'Can we use AI to generate Form 3CD for a client with ₹47 crore turnover?' What is the right answer?
questions.explanation: Form 3CD is signed by the auditor under Section 44AB. AI may draft sections, populate tables, even cross-check disclosures, but the signature, opinion, and responsibility are the auditor's. The 'never-ship rule' applies.

choices.label: AI can draft, populate, and cross-check, but the auditor signs the final form after a complete review — AI never produces the version that is filed
choices.explanation: Right. This is the never-ship rule. AI never produces the version that goes to the department.

choices.label: Yes — AI generates the form and the partner signs
choices.explanation: Signing without doing the work is professional misconduct under the Chartered Accountants Act.

choices.label: No — AI cannot help with tax audit work at all
choices.explanation: Wrong in the other direction. AI accelerates the boring 80 percent; the auditor does the 20 percent.

choices.label: Only if the client signs a waiver
choices.explanation: A client waiver does not affect the auditor's statutory responsibility.

questions.stem: What is an 'eval log' in the context of an AI-assisted accounting workflow?
questions.explanation: An eval log records, for each AI run, what was given, what came back, who reviewed it, what changed, and the model version. This is the audit trail equivalent for AI work.

choices.label: A timestamped record of prompt, context documents, model version, response, reviewer name, and any corrections — preserved for the audit period
choices.explanation: Yes. If you cannot answer 'who, when, with what, and what changed' for any AI output, you do not have an audit trail.

choices.label: ChatGPT's chat history
choices.explanation: Chat history is not retained reliably and cannot be audited. It is not a substitute.

choices.label: A monthly bill from the AI vendor
choices.explanation: Cost is not the same as an audit trail.

choices.label: Notes the CA writes after the engagement
choices.explanation: Useful, but not enough. The eval log records the AI's actual inputs and outputs, not your summary.

questions.stem: Your client sent the purchase register as a 47-tab Excel with merged cells, hand-written notes in column F, and three rows of 'TOTAL' in different fonts. You want AI to parse it. What is the **first** thing you do?
questions.explanation: The 'looks like a poem' problem. AI is great at messy data, but you give it the cleanest input you can produce. Standardise the structure first, then prompt.

choices.label: Flatten and standardise the data into one rectangular sheet with consistent headers before feeding to AI
choices.explanation: Right. Garbage in, garbage out applies double for LLMs. Five minutes of manual cleanup saves an hour of wrong output.

choices.label: Feed the file to ChatGPT and hope
choices.explanation: This is how the 'AI ne bola looks like a poem' meme happens.

choices.label: Refuse the engagement
choices.explanation: The data is messy, not impossible. Do the work.

choices.label: Charge a higher fee and feed the file as-is
choices.explanation: Higher fees for worse work is not the model.

questions.stem: Which of these are appropriate uses of RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) for an Indian tax practice? **Select all that apply.**
questions.explanation: RAG works wherever you have a stable, knowable corpus the model should cite from rather than invent. Stable jurisprudence and bare acts qualify; client-specific judgment does not.

choices.label: Indexing the GST Act, CGST Rules, and CBIC notifications so the model cites them when answering classification questions
choices.explanation: Classic RAG use case. The model cites a real document; you can verify.

choices.label: Indexing your firm's past advisory notes so juniors can find precedents
choices.explanation: Internal knowledge base via RAG is a high-value use; tag confidence and require partner review for any opinion that flows to a client.

choices.label: Asking the model to 'use its training data' for the latest TDS rates without giving it the source
choices.explanation: Training data is stale and untraceable. This is the no-RAG anti-pattern.

choices.label: Letting the model decide whether a client's transaction is a 'royalty' under a tax treaty
choices.explanation: Treaty interpretation is a CA judgment call. RAG can surface the treaty text; the conclusion is yours.

questions.stem: Your AI-assisted reconciliation produced 1,847 matches, 142 of which the model marked 'low confidence' (below 70 percent). The partner wants the report by EOD. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Low-confidence matches are exactly where you spend the human hour. Skipping them defeats the entire purpose of confidence scoring.

choices.label: Manually review every low-confidence match and the top 20 by rupee value, even if it pushes the deadline by an hour
choices.explanation: Right. The whole point of confidence scoring is to concentrate human attention where it matters. Skipping the low-confidence reviews is the failure mode.

choices.label: Accept all 1,847 matches and ship
choices.explanation: You ignored the model's own warning. This is worse than not using AI at all.

choices.label: Re-run the AI with a different prompt until everything is high-confidence
choices.explanation: Pressure-cooking the model into false confidence does not change the underlying ambiguity.

choices.label: Hand the file back to the client and ask them to do it
choices.explanation: Probably not the deliverable they paid for.

questions.stem: Define the 'never-ship rule' in your own words.
questions.explanation: The never-ship rule says: AI never produces the final artefact that is filed, signed, or ships to the client. A CA always reviews and signs.

choices.label: AI may draft, format, and cross-check, but the version that is filed, signed, or sent to a client must be the result of a CA's review and signoff
choices.explanation: Yes. The boundary is at the artefact, not the workflow.

choices.label: Never use AI for any part of accounting
choices.explanation: Too restrictive; you give up the 80 percent.

choices.label: Never tell the client you used AI
choices.explanation: Wrong on ethics and on practice.

choices.label: Always use AI; never review
choices.explanation: The exact opposite.

questions.stem: An auditor at your firm is using AI to summarise a 340-page lease agreement to identify key obligations under Ind AS 116. Which of the following are **good practice**? **Select all that apply.**
questions.explanation: Source citation, sampling against the original, and CA judgment on classification are the discipline. Trusting summaries blindly is the failure mode.

choices.label: Asking the model to cite the page and clause for every obligation it lists
choices.explanation: Yes. If you cannot trace the summary back to the document, the summary is unverifiable.

choices.label: Sampling 10 random clauses and verifying the model summarised them correctly
choices.explanation: Sampling is the audit-grade check on the AI's accuracy.

choices.label: Letting the model decide whether the lease is 'short-term' under Ind AS 116
choices.explanation: Classification under Ind AS is a judgment call; auditor only.

choices.label: Skipping the original document entirely because the summary is good enough
choices.explanation: This is exactly what the discipline is designed to prevent.

questions.stem: A peer at another firm tells you they 'fully automated' GSTR-3B filing using AI for 200 SME clients. Your reaction?
questions.explanation: Fully automated filing crosses the never-ship rule. There is no defensible workflow that removes the CA from the signing of a statutory return.

choices.label: Concern — fully automated statutory filing without per-client CA signoff is a compliance and professional risk waiting to surface
choices.explanation: Right. The cost saving is real until the first wrong filing triggers a notice; then the firm and the client both pay.

choices.label: Admiration — that is the future of practice
choices.explanation: It may be the future of marketing copy. It is not the future of liability.

choices.label: Indifference — every firm chooses its risk appetite
choices.explanation: Statutory filings are not a personal preference. The risk lands on real people.

choices.label: You ask them to share their prompt
choices.explanation: The problem is not the prompt; it is the absence of a CA review tier.

questions.stem: You are pitching an AI-assisted bookkeeping retainer to a Bangalore restaurant chain with 14 outlets and roughly 9,000 transactions per month. Which sentence belongs in the proposal?
questions.explanation: The honest pitch describes the tiering, the human review tier, and the limits. Anything that promises 'AI-only' or 'fully automated' is overselling.

choices.label: AI categorises transactions and produces a confidence score; our team reviews every low-confidence entry and every transaction above ₹50,000; you receive the books with an AI-assist disclosure and CA signoff
choices.explanation: Honest, defensible, sellable. Names the tiering and the signoff.

choices.label: AI does your books — no human involvement, half the price
choices.explanation: Half the price, twice the risk; the first time a category is wrong on a tax-relevant entry, the savings vanish.

choices.label: We use AI but won't tell you because it is our secret sauce
choices.explanation: Disclosure is the floor of professional ethics in 2026.

choices.label: We do not use AI; everything is hand-keyed by articled assistants
choices.explanation: Probably true at higher cost and lower quality. The honest pitch acknowledges AI.

questions.stem: What is the right way to handle an AI-generated GST notification or section number that you cannot find on the CBIC site?
questions.explanation: If you cannot verify a citation against the source, you assume it is hallucinated. Do not file or advise based on it.

choices.label: Treat it as a hallucination and discard it; never file or advise based on a citation you cannot independently verify
choices.explanation: Yes. Verifiability is the floor; if a citation does not exist on the official site, it does not exist.

choices.label: Use it anyway; the model is usually right
choices.explanation: Usually-right is not a defence in front of an Assessing Officer.

choices.label: Ask three other LLMs and go with the majority
choices.explanation: Three models can hallucinate the same plausible answer; consensus is not verification.

choices.label: Email the client the citation as-is and let them figure it out
choices.explanation: You signed the engagement letter, not them.

project.title: Capstone: Scope an AI-Assisted GST Reconciliation Engagement for 47 SME Clients
project.prompt:
## The brief

You are a CA at a Pune firm. The senior partner forwards you an email from your largest enterprise client, an SME consortium that wants to consolidate their compliance work. The ask:

> *"We have 47 SME clients across our group. Each does roughly ₹2 to ₹15 crore in turnover. We've heard you can use AI to do the GST reconciliation. Quote for a monthly retainer covering GSTR-2A vs purchase register reconciliation, ITC claim recommendations, and GSTR-3B filing. Start next quarter. We want to cut our compliance cost by 40 percent."*

The partner adds, in the forward: *"Don't say no, but don't get us in trouble either. Send me a one-page scope by Monday."*

## What to deliver

Write a one-page scope (400 to 600 words) that covers:

1. **What AI does** — which parts of the workflow you delegate to AI, with named moves (classify-then-verify, confidence tiers, RAG against the GST Act, etc.). Be specific about the confidence thresholds.
2. **What stays human** — which parts a CA must do, and why (statutory signoff, ITC eligibility judgment, exception handling). Name the never-ship rule.
3. **Compliance guardrails** — eval log requirements, four-eye review, AI-assist disclosure to clients, audit trail retention, what happens when GSTR-2A is updated mid-month.
4. **Pricing and SLA** — defend the 40 percent cost reduction or push back honestly. Tell the partner what they get, what they don't, and what fails.
5. **The clarifying question you'd send the client first** — because the brief is under-specified (47 clients of what kind? Do they share an ERP? What's the current monthly cost?).

## What we're really testing

We care about how you scope under uncertainty, defend your AI choices, and where you draw the never-ship line. There is no single correct answer; there is a class of defensible answers and a class of indefensible ones.

## Constraints

- Indian regulatory context: CGST Act 2017, Section 16 ITC, Rule 36(4), GSTR-2A vs 2B, GSTR-3B.
- Don't promise what you cannot deliver. The partner can see through it; the client will too.
- Use specific numbers (confidence thresholds, rupee values, mismatch percentages, hours per client per month).

levels.label: Every AI delegation has a named guardrail (confidence tier, RAG citation, eval log, four-eye review). The never-ship rule is explicit. Indefensible practices (auto-filing, AI-only ITC decisions) are explicitly refused.
Most AI delegations have guardrails; the never-ship rule is mentioned but not defended; one questionable practice slips in.
Mentions AI handles 'most of the work' but does not name the moves; review tiers are vague.
Promises automation without limits; no review tiers; no never-ship rule.

Names at least 3 assumptions about the client (ERP standardisation, transaction volume, GSTR-2A timing, ITC dispute appetite) and how the scope changes if each is wrong. Includes the clarifying question.
Names 1 to 2 assumptions and includes the clarifying question.
Acknowledges uncertainty in the brief but does not enumerate assumptions.
Treats the brief as fully specified; no clarifying question.
One page, second-person, specific numbers (confidence thresholds, hours, rupee thresholds, % mismatch). Defends the price honestly. The partner can forward this to the client without rewriting.
Mostly clear; one or two soft places where the partner would need to rewrite a sentence.
Conceptually right but verbose or hedged; no specific numbers.
Marketing-speak. Could have been written by anyone about anything.

credential.title: AI for Accounting
credential.description: Holds the judgment to scope, run, and defend an AI-assisted accounting engagement under Indian compliance — knowing exactly what to delegate to AI and what only a CA may sign.
